note: Record regions, not countries. A region is a piece of ground whose records were filed the same way, and an era is a stretch of years over which that stayed true. The regime bands are the researched sovereignty of the Defranceski archive; what is new here is `filedUnder` — which archive a regime actually MEANS. That is the whole point: knowing Gračišće was Italian in 1930 is trivia until it tells you to open FamilySearch's Pola and Trieste collection rather than its Croatian one. The regions are chosen by where research is actually being done rather than by what would look impressive on a map. Each one was written because somebody was stuck on that ground and needed to know whose archive to write to. Each region now carries `alt`: the names a record actually uses for that ground — Kranjska and Krain and Krainburg for Carniola, Küstenland for Istria. A reader holding a 19th-century entry has the historical name, not the modern label, and until now typing it found nothing at all.
precision: The rings are approximate — deliberately. They exist to shade which filing system a place fell under, not to adjudicate a border. A place near a ring's edge should be checked against both neighbours.

dutch.label: Dutch — the Company and the Batavian Republic

galicia.label: Austria — Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria

boer.label: The Boer republics and the Voortrekker states

hre.label: Holy Roman Empire — the prince-bishoprics and imperial states

hesse.label: Hesse-Darmstadt — the Landgraviate, Grand Duchy and People's State

confed.label: German Confederation — the free cities and small states

navarre.label: Kingdom of Navarre within the Spanish crown

emilian.label: Duchies of Parma, Modena and the Este and Farnese lands

regions.label: Central Istria
regions.sub: Pazin, Gračišće, Gologorica, Lindar, Pićan

eras.note: No parish registers exist anywhere for this period. Trent required them only from 1563, and Istria's earliest surviving books are seventeenth-century.
The books stayed with the parish and were gathered to Pazin in the twentieth century. FamilySearch filmed them as Croatia, Church Books (collection 2040054).
The parish books continue unbroken; the regime change is invisible in them.
Parish registers to Pazin. The imperial press covering these years is in ANNO, and it names people the registers only number.

THE TRAP. Records of these years are filed under ITALY, not Croatia — FamilySearch's Italy, Pola and Trieste collection (2152685) holds Croatian parishes. Searching the Croatian collection alone finds nothing.
Civil registration is patchy. Arolsen holds the deportation and forced-labour records of these years.
Registration moves to the matični ured. Anything inside the hundred-year privacy cut-off is not public, whoever holds it.
Current registration is with the matični ured in Pazin. Not public.

regions.label: Southern Istria
regions.sub: Pula, Vodnjan, Rovinj, Svetvinčenat, Ližnjan

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Republic of Venice — Istria da Mar
eras.note: Venetian Istria, diocese of Pola. The registers are in Italian and Latin and the hands are Venetian.
Pula becomes the imperial navy's main port, and the population triples. Naval and garrison records are Viennese, not local.
Filed under Italy. FamilySearch collection 2152685 covers Buje, Novigrad, Oprtalj, Brtonigla and Materada among others.
The esodo: most of the Italian-speaking population leaves between 1945 and 1956. People vanish from these registers without dying.

regions.label: The Kvarner — Senj, Vinodol, Rijeka
regions.sub: Rijeka, Bakar, Crikvenica, Novi Vinodolski, Senj

eras.polity: Frankopan counts of Krk and Vinodol
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Habsburg — Senj a Military Frontier garrison
eras.note: THE TRAP. Senj was Militärgrenze, administered from Vienna and Graz, not from Croatia's civil counties. Military Frontier material is in the Croatian State Archive and in the Vienna Kriegsarchiv — not where a Croatian county search would look.

eras.polity: Austria–Hungary — Fiume a Hungarian corpus separatum
eras.note: THE TRAP. Rijeka/Fiume was governed from BUDAPEST, not Vienna or Zagreb, from 1779. Its administrative records are Hungarian — which is why Hungaricana finds them and Croatian catalogues sometimes do not.
The border ran through the town. Fiume was Italian and Sušak, across the Rječina, was Yugoslav — two filing systems, one city, for twenty-five years.

regions.label: Carnia, Friuli
regions.sub: Ovaro, Mione, Muina, Agrons — the Val Degano

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Republic of Venice — Patria del Friuli
eras.note: Parish registers only, kept by the parish and now largely with the diocese of Udine. There is no civil registration yet.
THE GOOD NEWS. Civil registration begins in 1806 — births, marriages and deaths recorded by the comune, in Italian, in a standard form. Antenati has the images, free and without an account.
Civil registration lapses; the parish register is the record again for these fifty years.
Civil registration resumes in 1871. Antenati holds Udine's, and FamilySearch filmed the same books as collection 1939238.

regions.label: Dalmatia
regions.sub: Split, Omiš, Trogir, Seget

eras.note: Before registers.
Venetian Dalmatia. Many parish books went to Zadar rather than Split, which is where a Split-only search fails.
Governed from Zadar, and its records went there.
A short Italian occupation with its own paperwork, easy to miss between two Yugoslav periods.

regions.label: The Imotski frontier
regions.sub: Imotski and the Zagora — the Venetian-Ottoman border

eras.note: THE HOLE. Two hundred years of Ottoman rule, and Catholic parish registers barely survive it. What exists for these years is Franciscan, held by the monasteries, and almost none of it is online.
Taken by Venice in 1717. Registers begin here, and effectively nowhere earlier.

regions.label: Campania — Caserta and Naples
regions.sub: Arienzo, Arpaia, Caserta, Naples

eras.note: Parish registers only, and only after the Council of Trent required them in 1563. They stayed with the parish and the diocesan archive; there is no civil registration to find because none was kept.

THE GOOD NEWS. Civil registration begins on the mainland in 1809 — births, marriages and deaths written by the comune on a printed form, in Italian, with the parents named and aged. Antenati has the images, free and without an account. This is the single best year in southern Italian genealogy.
The Bourbons came back and kept the French registers. The series runs unbroken through the restoration, which is not true of everything Napoleon started.
Antenati publishes to a hundred-year cut-off. Anything more recent is at the comune, and is not public.

regions.label: Eastern Sicily — Catania
regions.sub: Piedimonte Etneo, Catania, Acireale

eras.note: Parish registers only, kept by the parish and the diocese.

THE TRAP. Sicily's civil registration begins in 1820 — ELEVEN YEARS AFTER the mainland's 1809. A researcher who has worked in Campania and carries the 1809 date across the strait will hunt for a Sicilian birth record that was never written.

regions.label: Calabria
regions.sub: Briatico, Vibo Valentia, Tropea

eras.note: THE HOLE. The earthquake of 1783 levelled much of Calabria Ultra and burned or buried the comune and parish archives with it — Briatico itself was destroyed and rebuilt on a new site. For a great many Calabrian towns there is simply nothing before 1783, and no archive to write to about it.
Civil registration from 1809, as on the rest of the mainland.
The earthquakes of 1905 and 1908 took another bite out of the Calabrian registers. A gap here is more often a destroyed book than an unfilmed one.

regions.label: West Prussia
regions.sub: Danzig, Thorn, Graudenz, Marienwerder, Elbing

eras.note: Royal Prussia belonged to the Polish crown after the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466.
Prussia took most of the area in the First Partition of 1772 and made it a province in 1773; Danzig and Thorn joined in the Second Partition of 1793.

eras.polity: Napoleonic order — the Duchy of Warsaw and the Free City of Danzig
eras.note: The province lost its southern land to the Duchy of Warsaw; Danzig was a Free City from 1807 to 1814. The Congress of Vienna returned Danzig, Culm and Thorn in 1815.
Merged with East Prussia in 1829 as the Province of Prussia, and separated again in 1878.

eras.polity: Poland (the Corridor), the Free City of Danzig, and East Prussia
eras.note: The Treaty of Versailles of 1919 divided the territory: Danzig became a free city, the central region the Polish Corridor, the eastern area part of East Prussia, and the western part joined Posen in 1922 as Posen–West Prussia.
Nazi Germany absorbed the former province in 1939.
Restored to Poland under the Potsdam Agreement. Danzig is Gdańsk, Thorn is Toruń.

regions.label: Posen — Prussian Poland
regions.sub: Szubin (Schubin), Bydgoszcz (Bromberg), Poznań (Posen)

eras.note: Catholic parish registers in Latin, kept by the parish.
Napoleonic civil registration, kept by the parish priest acting as registrar — in Polish, and in a standard narrative form.
Three parallel series and a family can be in more than one: Catholic, Protestant and Jewish, each kept by its own congregation.

Civil registration by Standesamt from 1 OCTOBER 1874 — the date to remember for anywhere in Prussia. From then there is a state record for everyone regardless of religion, and the Polish state archives hold it.
Arolsen holds the deportation, forced-labour and displaced-persons records of these years.

THE TRAP. The German place names are gone, and the catalogues are in Polish. Schubin is SZUBIN, Bromberg is BYDGOSZCZ, Posen is POZNAŃ. The registers mostly stayed where they were and are held by the Polish state archives — but they are catalogued under the Polish name, so a search for Schubin returns nothing while the books sit in Bydgoszcz.

regions.label: The eastern Cape
regions.sub: Graaff-Reinet, Cradock, Somerset East

eras.polity: Dutch East India Company — Cape of Good Hope
eras.note: The Dutch Reformed Church register IS the record — baptism, marriage, and the opgaaf rolls. There is no civil registration and there will not be for two hundred years.

THE TRAP. There is no general civil registration of births and deaths at the Cape until 1895, and it stays patchy after. Hunting for a birth certificate is hunting for something nobody wrote. What names a family instead is the ESTATE FILE — the Master of the Supreme Court's MOOC series, indexed on NAAIRS — together with the Dutch Reformed Church register and the death notice inside the estate file, which lists the parents and the children.

regions.label: England and Wales
regions.sub: Chew Magna, Bristol, Chatham — and every English parish

eras.note: Thomas Cromwell ordered every parish to keep a register in 1538, and until 1837 it is the record. THE TRAP is where it lives: parish registers are held by COUNTY record offices, not nationally — Somerset's at Taunton, Kent's at Maidstone — and each licensed its images to a different commercial site.

Civil registration begins 1 JULY 1837. THE TRAP is that the GRO index gives you a reference, not a record: you order and pay for the certificate. FreeBMD indexes the same thing for nothing. And registration was not the parent's legal duty until 1875, so the first four decades are incomplete by design.

regions.label: Queensland
regions.sub: Brisbane, Ipswich, Toowoomba

eras.note: THE TRAP. Queensland did not exist before 6 JUNE 1859. A birth at Brisbane in 1850 is a NEW SOUTH WALES record, indexed by New South Wales, and searching Queensland's index for it returns nothing at all.
Civil registration from separation. Queensland's historical index is free to search and the certificates are charged.

Immigration, naturalisation and wartime alien registration are FEDERAL and are at the National Archives in Canberra, not with the state. For a European arrival those files are often fuller than anything the state holds.

regions.label: Buenos Aires
regions.sub: Buenos Aires, La Plata, Luján, Mercedes, Chascomús

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Governorate of the Río de la Plata
Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata
United Provinces, then the Argentine Confederation under Rosas
eras.note: Buenos Aires had long operated as a semi-independent state under Juan Manuel de Rosas, who was deposed at the Battle of Caseros in 1852.

Buenos Aires overthrew the Confederation's government on 11 September 1852 and governed itself under its own constitution of April 1854; it defeated the Confederation at Pavón in September 1861 and rejoined in December 1861.

regions.label: Santa Fe — Rosario
regions.sub: Rosario, Santa Fe

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata
eras.note: Catholic parish registers only, in Spanish, kept by the parish and now largely with the diocese.
Independence changes the flag and not the filing: the parish register is still the only record of a birth.

THE TRAP. Argentine civil registration is PROVINCIAL, not national, and Santa Fe's begins in 1889 — later than Buenos Aires. There is no national index to search and the national archive does not hold it: you must know which province, and then find that province's registry. FamilySearch filmed Santa Fe's.

regions.label: Galicia
regions.sub: Kraków, Tarnów, Przemyśl, Lwów (Lviv), Tarnopol (Ternopil)

eras.note: Before registers anywhere.
Roman Catholic registers in Latin, Greek Catholic in Cyrillic, kept by each parish.

eras.polity: Austria — Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria
eras.note: THE TRAP, AND IT IS A THREEFOLD ONE. From 1784 Austria made the parish priest the civil registrar and required THREE PARALLEL SERIES — Roman Catholic, Greek Catholic and Jewish — each kept by its own congregation. A family can appear in more than one and searching only the Roman Catholic books misses half of eastern Galicia. The Jewish series is JewishGen's ground, not the Catholic archives'.
Galician Jewry is destroyed in these years. Arolsen and Yad Vashem hold what the parish registers stopped recording.

eras.polity: Poland west of the San; Ukraine east of it
eras.note: THE SECOND TRAP. The border of 1945 cut Galicia in half and its archives with it. Records west of the San are at Przemyśl and Kraków; east of it they are at Lviv and Ternopil, in Ukraine, catalogued in another language under another system. One province, two countries, two catalogues, and no cross-reference between them.

regions.label: Bukovina
regions.sub: Czernowitz (Chernivtsi), Suceava, Rădăuți

eras.note: Orthodox monastery records, and almost nothing that survives as a register.

Registers in German and Romanian, in four parallel series — Orthodox, Roman Catholic, Greek Catholic and Jewish. Czernowitz was one of the most Jewish cities in Europe and its records are filed accordingly.
The deportations to Transnistria fall in these years. Yad Vashem holds the names.

eras.polity: Ukraine in the north; Romania in the south
eras.note: THE TRAP. The line drawn in 1940 still runs through Bukovina. Northern records are at Chernivtsi in Ukraine, southern at Suceava in Romania, and a family that never moved can have its baptism in one country and its marriage in the other.

regions.label: Bohemia
regions.sub: Prague, Plzeň, České Budějovice, Litoměřice

eras.note: Before registers.

THE GOOD NEWS, AND IT IS EXCEPTIONAL. The Czech regional archives have digitised nearly every surviving parish register and put them online free, without an account. Western Bohemia is at Porta fontium, the rest at the regional archives' own portals. This is the best-served ground in this entire map.
The Sudeten borderlands are annexed in 1938 and the interior occupied in 1939; the German population is expelled in 1945. The registers largely stayed.

regions.label: Moravia and Silesia
regions.sub: Brno, Olomouc, Opava, Ostrava

eras.note: Before registers.
Acta Publica has the Moravian and Silesian parish registers, free and without an account — the same exceptional provision as Bohemia.

regions.label: Prekmurje — the Hungarian Mur-land
regions.sub: Murska Sobota (Muraszombat), Lendava (Alsólendva), Beltinci, Turnišče, Tišina, Grad (Felsőlendva)

eras.polity: Kingdom of Hungary — Vas and Zala counties
eras.note: Before registers.
Hungarian genealogy very often stops at 1700 (see the Hungary region). This atlas holds no Prekmurje volume from before 1895, so for these centuries there is nothing here to point at.

eras.polity: Habsburg — Kingdom of Hungary, in Vas and Zala counties
eras.note: Parish registers resume, in Latin, kept by each congregation separately. The ground is split between two counties: FamilySearch's own tree files Tišina and Grad under Vas and Turnišče under Zala, so a Prekmurje family has to be looked for under the county its village was in.

CIVIL REGISTRATION FROM 1 OCTOBER 1895 — state-kept, in Hungarian, covering everybody regardless of religion (see the Hungary region). It is all this atlas holds for the area: every volume begins in 1895 or later and is filed by FamilySearch under «Slovenia, Prekmurje and Međimurje, Civil Registers, 1895-1918». Međimurje is in Croatia today, so that collection's country is only half the ground it covers.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia
eras.note: THE HINGE. Yugoslav forces took the ground in August 1919 and the Treaty of Trianon confirmed it in 1920. The Hungarian-kept registers end here; from this point a Prekmurje family is filed in Slovenia, in the Drava Banovina from 1929.

Hungarian forces occupied Prekmurje in April 1941 and Hungary annexed it, so these years are filed under Hungary again. It is one of the three occupation zones the Carniola region's 1941 era refers to.

eras.polity: Yugoslavia — the Socialist Republic of Slovenia

regions.label: Civil Croatia
regions.sub: Zagreb, Varaždin, Koprivnica, Bjelovar, Križevci

eras.polity: Kingdom of Croatia in personal union with Hungary
eras.note: The Kingdom of Croatia entered a personal union with Hungary in 1102.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Croatia under the Habsburg monarchy
Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia (within the Hungarian half)
eras.note: The Croatian–Hungarian Settlement of 1868 merged Croatia and Slavonia into the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia; the Military Frontiers were reincorporated in 1881.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia
eras.note: The Croatian Sabor proclaimed independence on 29 October 1918 and joined the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs; most of the territory became the Sava Banovina in 1929 and the autonomous Banovina of Croatia was created on 24 August 1939.

regions.label: Slavonia
regions.sub: Osijek, Požega, Đakovo, Vinkovci, Virovitica, Vukovar

eras.polity: Kingdom of Croatia in personal union with Hungary
eras.note: Slavonia became part of a personal union with Hungary in 1102.
The Ottomans held Osijek by 1540 and took Virovitica in 1552; the Habsburgs regained the region in the Great Turkish War of the 1680s and the Treaty of Karlowitz transferred it in 1699.

eras.polity: Habsburg — the Kingdom of Slavonia and the Military Frontier
eras.note: Full civil administration was introduced in the Kingdom of Slavonia in 1745; it was administratively part of both Croatia and Hungary.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia (within the Hungarian half)
eras.note: The Military Frontier was abolished in 1881.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia

eras.note: Eastern Slavonia was restored to Croatia under the Erdut Agreement, with the process completed in 1998.

regions.label: Western Istria
regions.sub: Poreč, Umag, Buje, Novigrad, Vrsar

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Republic of Venice — Istria da Mar
eras.note: Venetian Istria, diocese of Pola. The registers are in Italian and Latin and the hands are Venetian.
Pula becomes the imperial navy's main port, and the population triples. Naval and garrison records are Viennese, not local.
Filed under Italy. FamilySearch collection 2152685 covers Buje, Novigrad, Oprtalj, Brtonigla and Materada among others.
The esodo: most of the Italian-speaking population leaves between 1945 and 1956. People vanish from these registers without dying.

regions.label: Hungary — the Kingdom's core
regions.sub: Budapest, Debrecen, Szeged, Pécs

eras.note: Before registers.

THE HOLE. A hundred and fifty years of Ottoman occupation across the centre of the kingdom, and almost no parish register survives it. Hungarian genealogy very often simply stops at 1700 and the reason is here.
Parish registers resume, in Latin, kept by Catholic, Reformed, Lutheran, Orthodox and Jewish congregations separately.

CIVIL REGISTRATION FROM 1 OCTOBER 1895 — state-kept, in Hungarian, covering everybody regardless of religion. The single most useful date in Hungarian research, and the duplicate copies are at the national archives.

THE TRAP, AND IT IS THE LARGEST ON THIS MAP. Trianon in 1920 moved TWO THIRDS of the Kingdom of Hungary to Romania, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia. A village that was Hungarian in 1890 keeps its pre-1920 registers in Budapest AND its later ones in Bucharest, Bratislava or Belgrade — under a name that also changed.

regions.label: Transylvania and the Banat
regions.sub: Cluj (Kolozsvár), Brașov, Sibiu, Timișoara

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Principality of Transylvania, under Ottoman suzerainty
eras.note: Saxon Lutheran towns keep records earlier than most of the region; elsewhere very little survives.
Four recognised religions and a Romanian Orthodox majority, each keeping its own registers: Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist, Unitarian and Orthodox.
Civil registration from 1 October 1895, in Hungarian, whatever the family's language at home.

THE TRAP. Pre-1918 records are HUNGARIAN and largely at Budapest; post-1918 are ROMANIAN and at the county archives. A family in one village, unmoved, is filed in two countries and two languages either side of 1918 — and the village has a Hungarian name, a Romanian name and often a German one.

regions.label: East Prussia
regions.sub: Königsberg (Kaliningrad), Memel (Klaipėda), Allenstein (Olsztyn)

eras.note: Before registers.
Overwhelmingly Lutheran, so the church books are Protestant and Archion is the route to them.

eras.polity: German Empire — Province of East Prussia
eras.note: Civil registration by Standesamt from 1 OCTOBER 1874, as everywhere in Prussia.

eras.polity: Russia in the north; Poland in the south; Lithuania at Memel
eras.note: THE BIGGEST TRAP OF ALL, AND IT RUNS THE OTHER WAY. The population fled or was expelled and — unusually — MANY OF THE CHURCH REGISTERS WENT WEST WITH THEM. East Prussian Protestant registers are largely in Berlin and Leipzig, NOT in Kaliningrad. Looking for Königsberg records in Russia is the classic wasted year of German genealogy.

regions.label: Pomerania and Danzig
regions.sub: Stettin (Szczecin), Danzig (Gdańsk), Köslin (Koszalin)

eras.note: Before registers, and then barely after them.

eras.polity: Swedish Pomerania in the west; Brandenburg-Prussia in the east
eras.note: THE FORGOTTEN TRAP. Western Pomerania was SWEDISH from 1648 to 1815, so its administrative records of those years can be in Stockholm rather than Berlin or Szczecin — which almost nobody thinks to check.
Standesamt civil registration from 1 October 1874.
Danzig is neither German nor Polish between the wars but a League of Nations free city keeping its own registers.
THE TRAP, the same one as Posen. Stettin is SZCZECIN and Danzig is GDAŃSK; the registers mostly stayed and are catalogued under the Polish names, so a search for the German one finds nothing at all.

regions.label: Ireland — the whole island
regions.sub: Dublin, Cork, Belfast, Galway

eras.polity: Kingdom of Ireland, under the English crown
eras.note: Church of Ireland registers from 1634 where they survive; Catholic registers almost nowhere before 1750. The penal laws are the reason, and they are a records fact as much as a political one.

eras.polity: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
eras.note: The Catholic parish registers begin in earnest — the National Library's microfilms are free and cover nearly every parish. Protestant marriages registered from 1845.
Civil registration of all births, marriages and deaths from 1864, free and photographed on IrishGenealogy.ie. The 1901 and 1911 censuses survive in full and are free at the National Archives.

eras.polity: Irish Free State and Republic in the south; Northern Ireland in the six counties
eras.note: THE TRAP. On 30 June 1922 the Public Record Office in the Four Courts burned with almost every Irish census before 1901, most Church of Ireland registers deposited there, and the wills. Researchers are still told to «look for the census» — there is no census to look for. What survives is what was never sent in: the Catholic parish registers, PRONI's copies in the north, Griffith's Valuation, and the Tithe Applotment books. Start there, not with the census.

regions.label: Scotland
regions.sub: Edinburgh, Glasgow, Aberdeen, the Highlands

eras.note: Kept by the parish minister, and kept unevenly: some parishes run from 1553 and some begin in 1820. A gap in the OPRs is usually a gap in the keeping, not a lost volume.

THE TRAP, and it is a pleasant one. Scottish statutory certificates carry far more than English ones — a marriage names both mothers including maiden surnames, a death names both parents. The 1855 registers name more still, because the first year was over-ambitious and then cut back. If your family is Scottish, do not settle for an index entry.

regions.label: The Palatinate
regions.sub: Speyer, Kaiserslautern, Landau, Zweibrücken, Neustadt

eras.polity: Electoral Palatinate and the neighbouring states
eras.note: The Wittelsbachs ruled the Electoral Palatinate from 1214; the area was split among ecclesiastical states, secular principalities and free imperial cities.
French forces occupied the region in 1794; the department of Mont-Tonnerre was formed in 1797.

eras.polity: Bavaria — the Palatinate (the Rheinkreis, called Pfalz from 1835)
eras.note: Placed under Bavarian rule after the Napoleonic era.
French occupation authorities combined the Palatinate with other territories to form Rhineland-Palatinate (1947 in Wikipedia's article; 1946 in a note at its end).

regions.label: Alsace and Lorraine
regions.sub: Strasbourg, Colmar, Metz, Mulhouse

eras.polity: France — the Three Bishoprics and, from 1648, Alsace
eras.note: Parish registers in Latin and German, kept by the parish, in a Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed patchwork that survived the annexation.
État civil from 1792 in French, in the standard French decennial-table form. Free and photographed at all three departmental archives.

THE TRAP. The registers do not move and the language does. From 1871 the same volume in the same building is written in German, names are Germanised — Jean becomes Johann, Mulhouse becomes Mülhausen — and the indexes a French-speaking researcher searches will not match. A family that never left the village appears to vanish in 1871 and reappear in 1918.
French again, and the local law kept several German-era provisions, which is why Alsace-Moselle still has its own civil code today.
Annexed outright rather than occupied. The malgré-nous conscriptions and the expulsions fall here; Arolsen holds names for the camps and the forced labour.

regions.label: Silesia
regions.sub: Breslau (Wrocław), Kattowitz (Katowice), Opole, Opava

eras.note: Catholic and Lutheran registers in Latin and German, kept by the parish.

eras.polity: Prussia — Province of Silesia (Austrian Silesia stays Habsburg)
eras.note: THE TRAP. Frederick took most of Silesia in 1742 and left a strip — Austrian Silesia, around Opava and Těšín — with the Habsburgs. Two record systems, two languages of administration and two present-day countries, for a province people still name as one place.
Standesamt civil registration from 1 October 1874, in German, alongside the church books.

eras.polity: Divided — East Upper Silesia to Poland in 1922, the rest German; Těšín split with Czechoslovakia
eras.note: THE TRAP, again and worse. The 1921 plebiscite and the partition that followed cut Upper Silesia in two, and Těšín was cut a third way. Three archives now hold what one parish produced.
Auschwitz is in this region, in what the Germans had annexed as Ost-Oberschlesien. Arolsen and Yad Vashem hold the names.

eras.polity: Poland, and Czech Silesia in the south
eras.note: THE TRAP that catches everyone. The German population was expelled and the place names changed wholesale — Breslau is Wrocław, Waldenburg is Wałbrzych, Gleiwitz is Gliwice. Records made in German before 1945 sit in Polish archives under Polish names. Search the German name for the record and the Polish name for the archive.

regions.label: Livonia, Estonia and Courland
regions.sub: Riga, Tartu (Dorpat), Tallinn (Reval), Jelgava (Mitau)

eras.polity: Sweden in the north, the Duchy of Courland in the south
eras.note: Lutheran parish registers from the seventeenth century where they survive, kept in German by a Baltic German clergy over an Estonian- and Latvian-speaking peasantry.

THE TRAP, and it is a surname trap. Serfdom ended here in 1816–1819, decades before the rest of the empire, and the peasantry had no hereditary surnames until then. Estonian and Latvian surnames were ISSUED between 1822 and 1835, parish by parish, often by the manor. Before that date your family has a first name and a farm name and nothing else, and no amount of searching a surname will find them.
Civil registration begins, and the 1935 Latvian census is a full household listing. Baltic German names are Estonianised and Latvianised in these years, by choice and by campaign.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Estonian and Latvian SSRs, with a German occupation 1941–44
eras.note: The 1941 and 1949 deportations, and the Umsiedlung that took almost the entire Baltic German population to the Reich in 1939–41. If the family was German-speaking and disappears around 1939, it did not die; it was resettled, and Germany holds the file.
Estonia's Saaga is free and complete enough to be startling; Latvia's Raduraksti needs only an account.

regions.label: Congress Poland — the Russian partition
regions.sub: Warsaw, Łódź, Lublin, Kielce

eras.note: Church registers in Latin, kept by the parish, as before the partition.

The Napoleonic Code arrives, and with it civil registration — kept by the parish priest acting as a civil registrar, in a long narrative paragraph rather than a column. These are the most informative Polish records there are.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Poland, in personal union with Russia
eras.note: The Napoleonic long-form register continues, in POLISH from 1826 and in separate volumes per denomination. Jewish civil registers begin as their own series in 1826 and are the single best source for Jewish Poland.

THE TRAP. From 1868 the registers are written in RUSSIAN, in Cyrillic, and they stay that way until 1918. The same parish, the same priest, the same form — in an alphabet most researchers cannot read and most indexes transliterate inconsistently. A family that seems to end in 1868 has not ended.
Polish again.

eras.polity: The General Government and the annexed western districts
eras.note: The ghettos, the camps and the near-total destruction of Jewish Poland fall here. Yad Vashem and Arolsen are the name sources; the Polish civil registers of these years are often the only paper a person left.
Registers pass to the state archives after 100 years for births and 80 for marriages and deaths; anything more recent is at the local Urząd Stanu Cywilnego and is not online.

regions.label: Carniola and the Slovene lands
regions.sub: Ljubljana (Laibach), Maribor (Marburg), Celje, Novo mesto

eras.note: Catholic parish registers in Latin, kept by the parish, from the later sixteenth century where they survive.

From 1784 the registers become a state instrument in a fixed columnar form, with house numbers. That house number is the key to the Franciscean cadastre and to the land records, and it is the most under-used field in Habsburg genealogy.
French civil registration for four years, in the Napoleonic form, before the Habsburgs take it back.

eras.polity: Austria — the Duchy of Carniola and Lower Styria
eras.note: Registers in Latin and German; the parish keeps the original and the diocese holds a copy, which is why a burned parish is not always a lost record.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia
eras.note: THE TRAP. The 1920 border left a quarter of the Slovene population inside ITALY — the Julian March, from Gorizia to Postojna — where their records were kept in Italian and their names were Italianised by decree. A Slovene family from Idrija or Postojna is filed under Italy for these years.

eras.polity: Partitioned between Germany, Italy and Hungary
eras.note: Three occupiers, three filing systems, and the deportations of Slovene families from the German zone.

eras.polity: Yugoslavia — the Socialist Republic of Slovenia
eras.note: Civil registration is taken from the church and given to the municipality in 1946. Registers after that date are at the občina, not the archive.
SIRAnet searches the finding aids of all six regional archives at once, which is the single most useful thing about Slovenian research.

regions.label: Serbia (Šumadija and the Morava)
regions.sub: Belgrade, Šabac, Valjevo, Kragujevac, Kruševac

eras.note: The Treaty of Passarowitz (21 July 1718) gave the Habsburgs the land south of the Sava and Danube, with Belgrade as capital; the Treaty of Belgrade (18 September 1739) returned it to the Ottomans.
The Orašac Assembly elected Karađorđe to lead the uprising in 1804.
Ottoman rule was restored in October 1813, until the Second Serbian Uprising of 1815.
The Ottomans recognised the state in the 1830 Hatt-i Sharif; the last Ottoman garrison left Belgrade Fortress in 1867 and the Treaty of Berlin (1878) gave international recognition.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia
German military administration — Territory of the Military Commander in Serbia
eras.note: German military administration began on 22 April 1941; a German-controlled puppet Government of National Salvation under Milan Nedić was set up on 29 August 1941; the territory was liberated on 20 October 1944.

regions.label: Bosnia and Herzegovina
regions.sub: Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Mostar, Tuzla

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire — the Eyalet, then Vilayet, of Bosnia
eras.note: No parish registers as such for most of this period. What exists is Ottoman: the defter tax surveys, the sicil court registers, and the vakuf endowment records — household by household, in Ottoman Turkish, and almost none of it indexed by name.

THE TRAP, and it is a filing trap. Occupied in 1878 but not annexed until 1908, Bosnia was administered by the joint Imperial finance ministry in VIENNA rather than by Austria or by Hungary. Its paper is therefore in neither national series — look in the Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv and in Sarajevo, not in Budapest.
Registers now kept in four parallel confessional series — Catholic, Orthodox, Muslim and Jewish — which is the form they keep for the rest of the century.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia

eras.note: Jasenovac falls in these years. Yad Vashem holds names for the Jewish and Roma victims; the Serb victims are less completely recorded anywhere.

eras.polity: Yugoslavia — the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina
eras.note: Registration passes to the municipality in 1946.

THE TRAP nobody wants to write down. The 1992–95 war destroyed municipal register offices, and reconstructed registers were rebuilt from testimony and from surviving copies. A post-war extract may be a reconstruction rather than a transcription, and it is worth asking which.

regions.label: Vojvodina and the Banat frontier
regions.sub: Novi Sad (Újvidék), Subotica (Szabadka), Zrenjanin, Sombor

eras.note: Frontier ground, depopulated and repopulated repeatedly. Almost nothing survives as a register.

eras.polity: Habsburg Hungary and the Military Frontier
eras.note: THE TRAP, and it is the reason this region needs its own entry. The Military Frontier was administered from VIENNA by the war ministry, not from Buda by the Hungarian county — so a family in a Grenzer village has military records where its neighbours ten kilometres away have county ones. The eighteenth-century resettlement brought German, Hungarian, Serb, Slovak and Romanian colonists into the same district, each with their own parish and their own language of register.

eras.polity: Austria-Hungary — the Voivodeship, then Hungarian counties
eras.note: Hungarian state civil registration from 1 October 1895, in Hungarian, alongside the confessional registers.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia
eras.note: THE TRAP for anyone searching by name. Hungarian-language registers to 1918, Serbian after, and the same person is written Kovács in one volume and Ковач in the next.

eras.polity: Partitioned — Hungary in the north, German Banat, Croatia in the west
eras.note: The Novi Sad raid of January 1942 and the deportation of the Jewish population fall here.

eras.polity: Yugoslavia, then Serbia — the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina
eras.note: The German-speaking population — the Donauschwaben, there since the 1720s — was expelled or interned in 1944–48. Their records stay; they do not.

regions.label: Quebec and French North America
regions.sub: Québec, Montréal, Trois-Rivières, the Acadian shore

eras.note: The most completely recorded population in the early modern Americas. Catholic parish registers were kept in DUPLICATE from the start — one copy to the parish, one to the civil court — so a burned parish is very rarely a lost record. Continuous from 1621.

eras.polity: British North America — the Province of Quebec, then Lower Canada
eras.note: The conquest changes the sovereign and not the registers. The Quebec Act of 1774 left French civil law and the Catholic Church in place, and the parish register goes on being the civil register, in French, in the same duplicate form.
Still the parish register doing civil duty, and still in duplicate. The Drouin microfilms photographed the lot.

eras.polity: Canada — civil registration by the state
eras.note: From 1994 the Directeur de l'état civil registers births, marriages and deaths, and the three-and-a-half-century run of parish registers as civil records ends. Records after 1994 are not in the archives.

regions.label: Acadia — the Maritimes
regions.sub: Port-Royal (Annapolis Royal), Halifax, Louisbourg, Île Saint-Jean

eras.note: Catholic parish registers from Port-Royal, thin and interrupted — the colony changed hands between France and England seven times before 1713.

eras.polity: Britain — Nova Scotia; France keeps Île Royale and Île Saint-Jean
eras.note: THE TRAP, in two halves. Mainland Acadia became British in 1713 and its people did not move; Cape Breton and Prince Edward Island stayed French until 1758 and 1763. Same families, same generation, two sovereigns and two archives.

THE TRAP for every Acadian line. The deportation scattered the population to the thirteen colonies, to England, to France, to Saint-Domingue and eventually to Louisiana. A family that vanishes from Nova Scotia in 1755 is not dead and is not in Nova Scotia — look in the Massachusetts town records, in the Poitou and Belle-Île registers in France, and in the Louisiana church registers from 1765.

eras.polity: Britain — Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island
eras.note: Acadians permitted to return, to different land. The Loyalist influx after 1783 doubles the population again and brings a second body of American records with it.
Provincial civil registration from the 1860s onward, each province on its own timetable.

regions.label: The Military Frontier — Vojna krajina
regions.sub: Lika, Kordun, Banija, the Slavonian frontier, Srijem

eras.polity: Habsburg military frontier, under Graz and Vienna
eras.note: The frontier was carved out of Croatia and Slavonia and put under the war council, not the ban. Catholic registers begin after Trent where a parish survived at all; the Orthodox settlers granted the Statuta Valachorum kept their own. Very little of either survives from before 1700.

THE TRAP, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS REGION EXISTS. From 1746 a frontier village belonged to its REGIMENT, not to a county. Its vital registers were kept by the regimental chaplain and filed under the regiment — Ogulin, Otočac, Slunj, Gradiška, Brod, Petrovaradin — so a search of the county archive for a Lika village finds nothing before 1881, and nothing is not the same as not existing. Look for the regiment.

The frontier was wound down over thirty years and abolished by degrees; the regimental series end at different dates in different districts, which is why a family can vanish from one series a decade before its neighbours do.
The frontier is incorporated into Croatia-Slavonia and its ground finally files like everywhere else: civil registration from 1895, county and parish series thereafter.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes; Yugoslavia
eras.note: Parish registers continue; the state registers of 1895 onward are held by the registry offices and pass to the state archives after a century.
Records of these four years are scattered and incomplete, and much of the Orthodox parish record of this ground was destroyed with the communities that kept it.
Church registers were gathered into the state archives; civil registration is with the matični ured of each municipality.
ARHiNET is the catalogue of the Croatian state archives and is the place to establish what survives before writing.

regions.label: The Netherlands
regions.sub: Holland, Utrecht, Gelderland, Brabant, Limburg, Friesland

eras.note: Before the state counted anybody, the churches did: the DTB books — doop, trouw, begraaf — kept by the Reformed church, and separately by Catholic, Lutheran, Mennonite and Jewish congregations. They are in the provincial and municipal archives, not in one national series, and a family that changed church changes book.

THE HINGE OF DUTCH RESEARCH. Civil registration — the burgerlijke stand — starts with the French, and the date differs by where you are: 1796 in the parts annexed early, in Limburg and Zeeuws-Vlaanderen, and 1811 for most of the country. Before that date there is no state record of a birth, only a baptism.

Civil registration continues unbroken and is indexed almost completely on WieWasWie, free. The population registers from 1850 are the other half of it: they follow a household from address to address, which is how a family is traced between the ten-yearly certificates.

The civil registers survive; the population registers were used to find people, and the Amsterdam registry was bombed by the resistance in 1943 for that reason. Arolsen holds the records of those deported.
Certificates become public after 100 years for births, 75 for marriages and 50 for deaths, so the open end of the series moves forward every January.

regions.label: Denmark
regions.sub: Jutland, Funen, Zealand, Bornholm, southern Jutland

eras.note: Parish registers were ordered in 1645 and most begin considerably later; what survives before 1700 is thin and local. They are at the Rigsarkivet and free to read as images on Arkivalieronline.

eras.polity: Denmark, after the loss of Norway
eras.note: From 1814 every parish keeps TWO registers, the minister's and the parish clerk's, held separately — so a fire or a gap in one is very often survivable in the other. This is the single most useful fact about Danish records and it is rarely mentioned.

eras.polity: Prussia, then the German Empire — in Schleswig only
eras.note: THE TRAP. Denmark lost Schleswig and Holstein in 1864, so a family from southern Jutland has German Prussian civil registration — Standesamt records from 1874 — for these years, not Danish ones, and the paper may be in Germany. North Schleswig voted itself back to Denmark in 1920; the records of the German period did not all follow.
The censuses of 1787, 1801, 1834, 1840, 1845, 1850 and onwards are digitised and indexed, and they are the fastest way into a Danish family before the registers are readable.

regions.label: Norway
regions.sub: Oslo, Bergen, Trondheim, Tromsø, the western fjords

eras.note: Norway was governed from Copenhagen and its parish registers follow the Danish pattern; the oldest surviving book is from the 1620s and most parishes begin after 1688. All of it is free, photographed and largely indexed on Digitalarkivet.

eras.polity: Norway in union with Sweden, with its own constitution
eras.note: The union did not move the paper: Norwegian records stayed Norwegian throughout and are at the Riksarkivet in Oslo and the eight regional state archives. The censuses of 1801, 1865, 1875, 1891 and 1900 are complete and free.

Parish registers remain the civil record until 1983. The emigrant lists from the ports — Oslo, Bergen, Trondheim — are on Digitalarkivet too, and they are where a family that left for America stops being Norwegian and starts being American.

regions.label: Sweden
regions.sub: Stockholm, Skåne, Småland, Dalarna, Norrland

eras.note: The church law of 1686 is why Swedish research works. It required every parish to keep births, marriages and deaths AND the husförhörslängd — the clerical survey, a household-by-household record of who lived where, re-made every few years, with literacy and moves noted. No other country in Europe has anything like it at that date.

The great emigration: roughly a fifth of the population left, most for America, and the parish out-migration books record where each of them said they were going. That line is usually the only bridge between a Swedish parish and an American county.

Civil registration passed from the church to the state in 1991; the parish books run to that date. Riksarkivet's own images are partly free and partly behind a subscription, which is why this ground is not coloured as open.

regions.label: Finland
regions.sub: Helsinki, Turku, Vyborg, Ostrobothnia, Karelia

eras.polity: Sweden — the eastern half of the realm
eras.note: Finland was not a Swedish possession but a part of Sweden, so the 1686 church law and its communion books apply here too and Finnish parish records are as good and as early as Swedish ones.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Finland, under the Russian crown
eras.note: Russia took Finland in 1809 and changed almost nothing about how it kept records: the Lutheran parishes went on keeping the same books in the same way. A researcher who assumes Russian imperial record-keeping here will look for the wrong thing.

THE TRAP IS KARELIA. The parishes ceded to the Soviet Union in 1940 and 1944 were evacuated, and their registers were evacuated with them — so the records of a place now in Russia are in Finland, at the National Archives, and not where the place is.
Parish registers are the civil record until 1999. The National Archives' own service is free; the Genealogical Society's index of it is the usual way in.

regions.label: Portugal
regions.sub: Lisbon, Porto, Braga, Coimbra, the Alentejo, the Algarve

eras.note: Trent required parish registers from 1563 and Portuguese parishes obeyed early, so the baptism books of the north can reach the sixteenth century. They are held by the DISTRICT archives, one per district, and digitised district by district on DigitArq rather than in one national series.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Portugal — after the civil war
eras.note: The religious orders were dissolved in 1834 and their archives went to the state, which is where monastic and diocesan material sits today. Parish registers continue as the only record of a birth.

Civil registration begins with the Republic in 1911 and is compulsory from then; before it, there is no state record and the parish book is the record. Registers pass to the district archive after a hundred years, so the open end moves each year.

regions.label: Belgium and the Southern Netherlands
regions.sub: Antwerp, Brussels, Ghent, Bruges, Liège, Namur, Hainaut, Limburg

eras.note: Parish registers begin after Trent and the good ones reach the sixteenth century. They are the ONLY record of a birth for the next two hundred years — there is no state register behind them.

The sovereign changes and the record-keeping does not: the parish goes on keeping the book. A researcher looking for an Austrian imperial series for these years is looking for something that was never created.

THE HINGE OF BELGIAN RESEARCH. France annexes the ground in 1795 and civil registration — the état civil, births, marriages and deaths recorded by the commune — begins in 1796. Before that date there is no state record of a birth anywhere in the country, only a baptism. After it there are two independent series for every person, which is why Belgian research is unusually tractable.
Fifteen years under The Hague, and the civil registers run unbroken through them. Material of these years can sit on either side of a border that did not exist yet.

THE TRAP IS THAT THERE IS NO CENTRAL ARCHIVE TO WRITE TO. The State Archives keep the registers in provincial repositories — Antwerp, Beveren, Bruges, Ghent, Hasselt, Kortrijk, Leuven, Liège, Mons, Namur, Tournai, Arlon, Eupen — and a request addressed to Brussels for a parish in Limburg goes to the wrong building. The population registers, kept by the commune from 1846, follow a household from address to address and are the other half of the work.
The civil registers continue under occupation. The deportation and forced-labour records of these years are a separate series and largely elsewhere.
Eupen-Malmedy passes from Germany to Belgium in 1920, so a family from that ground has German civil registration before it and Belgian after, and the paper did not all follow the border.
Arolsen holds the records of those deported from this ground.

Registers pass to the State Archives once they are old enough to be public, so the open end of the series moves forward year by year; check the current threshold with the repository rather than assuming it. Statbel publishes surnames by commune, which this atlas carries and which nothing else here has at that grain.

regions.label: The western Cape
regions.sub: Cape Town, Stellenbosch, Paarl, Swellendam, Worcester

eras.polity: Dutch East India Company — Cape of Good Hope

regions.label: The Transvaal
regions.sub: Pretoria, Johannesburg, Potchefstroom, Rustenburg, Lydenburg

eras.note: The Sand River Convention of 17 January 1852 recognised Boer independence north of the Vaal; the first president took office in 1857 and the 1858 constitution fixed the name.
Annexed by Britain on 12 April 1877; the Pretoria Convention of 3 August 1881 restored self-government.
Under British suzerainty until the London Convention of 27 February 1884; British forces occupied the republic after the Second Boer War began on 11 October 1899.
The Treaty of Vereeniging of 31 May 1902 ended the republic; limited self-government came in 1906–07.

eras.polity: Union of South Africa — Province of the Transvaal

regions.label: Natal
regions.sub: Durban, Pietermaritzburg, Ladysmith, Newcastle, Vryheid

eras.note: The Boers took control of Port Natal in May 1838; Wikipedia's infobox dates the republic 1839–1843.

eras.polity: Natal — British colony, administered from the Cape from 1844

eras.note: Natal became a distinct colony with its own legislative council in 1856, had responsible government by 1893, and Zululand was annexed to it in 1897.

eras.polity: Union of South Africa — Province of Natal

regions.label: The Orange Free State
regions.sub: Bloemfontein, Kroonstad, Bethlehem, Harrismith, Smithfield

eras.note: The Bloemfontein Convention of 23 February 1854 recognised the republic; Britain annexed it in 1900 during the Second Boer War.
Self-government came in 1907.

eras.polity: Union of South Africa — Province of the Orange Free State

regions.label: Trentino
regions.sub: Trento, Rovereto, Riva del Garda, Cles, Pergine

eras.note: A state of the Holy Roman Empire from 1027; the Council of Trent met there in 1545–1563.

eras.polity: Principality of Trent, under the County of Tyrol
eras.note: Secularised in 1803 and placed under the Habsburg County of Tyrol.
Bavaria annexed Trent together with Tyrol under the Peace of Pressburg.

eras.polity: Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy — Department of Alto Adige
eras.note: Bavaria ceded southern Tyrol in the Treaty of Schönbrunn of 14 October 1809; the change took effect on 10 June 1810.
Back under the Austrian crown land of Tyrol until the First World War.
Italy occupied the area in 1918 and the 1919 Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye formally ceded it.

regions.label: The Veneto
regions.sub: Venice, Padua, Verona, Vicenza, Treviso, Belluno

eras.note: Venice took Treviso and Bassano del Grappa in 1339; the fall of the Carrara of Padua is dated 1406.
The Treaty of Campo Formio gave Venice to Austria on 17 October 1797.
Gained by the Treaty of Pressburg of 26 December 1805; Venetia's annexation was announced on 30 March 1806 and ratified on 1 May.
The kingdom was formally established on 9 June 1815. Venice was an independent republic from 22 March 1848 until Austria retook it on 24 August 1849.
The Treaty of Vienna of 12 October 1866 ceded Venetia to France, which handed it to Italy on 19 October; a plebiscite on 21–22 October confirmed it.

regions.label: Lazio (the Papal heartland)
regions.sub: Rome, Viterbo, Frosinone, Velletri, Anagni

eras.note: Rome and the surrounding Duchy of Rome became part of the Papal States in 756, after the Donation of Pepin.
Declared in February 1798 by General Berthier; Neapolitan troops ended it in October 1799.
Papal rule was formally restored in June 1800 after a French reoccupation.
Napoleon annexed the rest of the Papal States, including Rome, on 17 May 1809.
Restored by the Congress of Vienna. A Roman Republic was declared in February 1849 and suppressed by French forces; Lazio was the only former papal territory still under the pope after March 1861.
Italian forces captured Rome on 20 September 1870 and a plebiscite in October annexed it.

regions.label: Frankfurt am Main
regions.sub: Frankfurt, Höchst, Bockenheim

eras.note: An Imperial Free City from 1372, directly subordinate to the Emperor.

eras.polity: Napoleonic order — Principality, then Grand Duchy, of Frankfurt
eras.note: Napoleon gave the city to Dalberg in 1806; the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt, formed in 1810, lasted until 1813.
The Congress of Vienna restored it as a sovereign city-state; the civic oath followed in 1816.
Occupied by Prussia on 16 July 1866 and annexed by decree on 20 September.

regions.label: Hesse-Darmstadt
regions.sub: Darmstadt, Giessen, Offenbach, Friedberg, Michelstadt

eras.note: Before 1806 the territory was the Landgraviate of Hesse-Darmstadt, part of the Holy Roman Empire.

Raised to a grand duchy on 13 August 1806 in Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine; it joined the German Confederation in 1815, took the name Hesse and by Rhine in 1816, lost the territory north of the Main in 1866 and joined the German Empire in 1871.
Replaced the grand duchy on 9 November 1918.

regions.label: Rhenish Hesse
regions.sub: Mainz, Worms, Bingen, Alzey, Oppenheim

eras.note: Formed in 1797 when France annexed the west bank of the Rhine, with Mainz as its capital.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Hesse — Rhenish Hesse
eras.note: After Napoleon's defeat in 1814 the department was divided between Bavaria and Hesse; the Congress of Vienna gave Hesse Rhenish Hesse, including the fortress of Mainz.

regions.label: Uruguay (the Banda Oriental)
regions.sub: Montevideo, Colonia, Canelones, Maldonado, Paysandú

eras.note: Spain and Portugal competed for the Banda Oriental; Montevideo was founded in 1726.
José Gervasio Artigas led revolts against Spanish rule from 1811. Who held the ground in these years was contested, and this era is a placeholder for that.
A Portuguese-Brazilian invasion in 1816 absorbed the territory as the Cisplatina province.
The Thirty-Three Orientals rebelled in 1825, setting off the Cisplatine War.
A British-mediated treaty in 1828 recognised Uruguay as an independent buffer state.
The first constitution followed in 1830.

regions.label: The Kingdom of Granada — Granada, Málaga, Almería
regions.sub: Granada, Málaga, Almería, San Pedro Alcántara

eras.note: Before Castilian rule and before the parish registers of Trent. Ibn al-Ahmar was declared emir on 16 July 1232 and made Granada his capital after 17 April 1238; the emirate roughly matched the modern provinces of Granada, Almería and Málaga and was often tributary to Castile. Málaga fell after a siege of May to August 1487 (its inhabitants were killed or enslaved), Almería and Guadix surrendered after Baeza fell in November 1489, and Granada was surrendered on 2 January 1492 (treaty of 25 November 1491).

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — Kingdom of Granada
eras.note: Muslims of the emirate were given the choice of expulsion or conversion after the uprising of 1499–1501; those who converted are the Moriscos. The Real Chancillería, the high court for the territory south of the Tagus, moved from Ciudad Real to Granada in 1505, and its documentary holdings are kept in the Archivo de la Real Chancillería de Granada. Parish registers: Trent requires them from 1545/1563.

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — Kingdom of Granada, repopulated after the Alpujarras revolt
eras.note: THE TRAP for the Alpujarras. The Morisco revolt ran from 24 December 1568 to March 1571; about 80,000 Moriscos (roughly half) were expelled from the kingdom, those from the Almería region by galley to Seville, and from 1571 settlers from western Andalusia, Galicia, Castile, Valencia, Murcia and the northern mountains were brought in to repopulate. A family in these villages after the 1570s may therefore come from outside Granada, and the surviving Moriscos were later expelled from Spain in 1609–1614. The end date 1833 is the year of the national provincial division (Javier de Burgos); that it ended the Kingdom of Granada as such is not established here. After 1834 the Audiencia Territorial de Granada covered Granada, Almería, Jaén and Málaga.

eras.polity: Spain — provinces of Granada, Málaga and Almería
eras.note: Parish registers stay the main record until civil registration; the old ones are in the diocesan archive.

Civil registration of births, marriages and deaths begins on 1 January 1871 (law of 17 June 1870; one source gives 1869). The records stay in each municipality, and some municipios hold civil records from as early as 1837.

eras.polity: Spain divided — Granada Nationalist, Málaga and Almería Republican
eras.note: THE FRONT RAN THROUGH THE REGION. Granada's garrison rose on 20 July 1936 and the rebels held the whole city by nightfall on 23 July; the Málaga province stayed under government control and Almería remained faithful to the Republic; Ronda fell on 16 September 1936; Nationalist troops entered Málaga on 8 February 1937 after the battle of 3–8 February; Almería was taken on 31 March 1939. Civil War losses of records are recorded for Spain; how far they reach this area is not established here.
Under Franco's State.
Under the Constitution of 1978.

regions.label: Seville and the lower Guadalquivir — Sevilla, Jerez, Cádiz
regions.sub: Sevilla, Jerez de la Frontera, Cádiz

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — Seville and Jerez
eras.note: Before parish registers. Ferdinand III besieged Seville from 1247 and the city surrendered on 23 November 1248; the terms contemplated evicting the population, and a mass exodus is suggested. Jerez surrendered to Castile in 1261 with its Muslim population remaining, which rebelled and was finally defeated in 1264.

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — Seville, port of the Indies trade
eras.note: THE TRAP for emigrants. The Casa de Contratación, which licensed emigrants to the Americas, was founded in Seville in 1503; its archive is held in the Archivo General de Indias in Seville. Parish registers: Trent requires them from 1545/1563, held in diocesan archives.

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — the Casa moved to Cádiz
eras.note: The Casa de Contratación moved to Cádiz in 1717 under the Bourbons and was abolished in 1790. The Archivo General de Indias was created in Seville by a decree approved by Charles III in February 1785, to gather Indies papers held at Simancas, Cádiz and Seville. The end date 1833 is the national provincial division (Javier de Burgos); its effect on this ground is not established here.

eras.polity: Spain — provinces of Seville and Cádiz
eras.note: Parish registers stay the main record until civil registration; the old ones are in the diocesan archive.

Civil registration of births, marriages and deaths begins on 1 January 1871 (law of 17 June 1870; one source gives 1869). The records stay in each municipality, and some municipios hold civil records from as early as 1837.

eras.polity: Spain — Nationalist zone from the first days
eras.note: Seville's garrison revolted on 18 July 1936 under General Queipo de Llano, and the rebels secured control by the afternoon of 22 July; the garrisons of Cádiz and Jerez revolted on the afternoon of 18 July. Jerez airport was built by the Nationalists in 1937 during the war. Civil War losses of records are recorded for Spain; how far they reach this area is not established here.
Under Franco's State.
Under the Constitution of 1978.

regions.label: Murcia and the south-east — Murcia, Cartagena, Hellín
regions.sub: Murcia, Cartagena, Mazarrón, La Unión, Hellín

eras.polity: Kingdom of Murcia — Treaty of Alcaraz to the Castilian annexation
eras.note: Before parish registers. Hellín was placed in the Kingdom of Murcia by the Treaty of Alcaraz of 1243. A Mudéjar revolt of 1264–1266 brought conquest by Aragon and the return of the territory to Castile, and 1266 is the start of the Kingdom of Murcia as a Castilian realm; how the ground was governed in between is not established here.

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — Kingdom of Murcia
eras.note: THE TRAP for Hellín. Hellín belonged to the Kingdom of Murcia (a Castilian realm 1266–1833), passed to the lordship of Juan Manuel, and returned to royal jurisdiction after the Marquesado wars of 1476–1480; in 1833 the kingdom was abolished by Javier de Burgos's provincial division and Hellín went to the new province of Albacete, so a search confined to the modern Region of Murcia does not reach it. Parish registers: Trent requires them from 1545/1563, held in diocesan archives.

eras.polity: Spain — Murcia province; Hellín in Albacete province
eras.note: Parish registers stay the main record until civil registration; the old ones are in the diocesan archive.

Civil registration of births, marriages and deaths begins on 1 January 1871 (law of 17 June 1870; one source gives 1869). The records stay in each municipality, and some municipios hold civil records from as early as 1837.

eras.polity: Spain — Republican rear until the Nationalist occupation of 31 March 1939
eras.note: The Nationalists occupied Albacete on 29 March 1939 and Almería, Murcia and Cartagena on 31 March; in Cartagena, Casado's supporters rose against Negrín's government on 4 March 1939 and were defeated on 7 March, and the Republican fleet sailed for Bizerte on 5 March. Who held each town in July 1936 is not established here. Civil War losses of records are recorded for Spain; how far they reach this area is not established here.
Under Franco's State.
Under the Constitution of 1978. Albacete province, including Hellín, passed in 1978 to the pre-autonomous body of Castilla-La Mancha, so Hellín lies outside the Region of Murcia.

regions.label: The Canary Islands — Lanzarote and the archipelago
regions.sub: San Bartolomé (Lanzarote) and the Canaries

eras.polity: Castilian conquest — lordships, then the Crown
eras.note: Before registers. Jean de Béthencourt and Gadifer de la Salle took Lanzarote in 1402 and Fuerteventura by 1405; rights passed among Castilian nobles from 1418, and in 1448 Maciot de Béthencourt sold the lordship of Lanzarote to Prince Henry of Portugal. The Crown conquered Gran Canaria (1478–1483), La Palma (to 3 May 1493) and Tenerife (to 25 July 1496, Treaty of Los Realejos). How Lanzarote was governed after 1477 is not established here.

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — the Canary Islands
eras.note: A separate Real Audiencia de Canarias was created in Gran Canaria in 1526, reducing the Granada Chancillería's jurisdiction. Parish registers: Trent requires them from 1545/1563, held in diocesan archives. On 30 November 1833 a single Province of Canary Islands was created, capital Santa Cruz de Tenerife.
Parish registers stay the main record until civil registration; the old ones are in the diocesan archive.

eras.polity: Spain — civil registration; two provinces from 1927
eras.note: Civil registration of births, marriages and deaths begins on 1 January 1871 (law of 17 June 1870; one source gives 1869). The records stay in each municipality, and some municipios hold civil records from as early as 1837. On 23 September 1927 the province was split into Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas.

eras.polity: Spain — Nationalist from July 1936; no war on the islands
eras.note: Franco, then General Commandant of the Canaries, joined the rising of 17 July 1936 and quickly took control of the archipelago, apart from resistance points on La Palma and in Vallehermoso on La Gomera; there was never a war on the islands. Post-war suppression of dissent was most severe there. Civil War losses of records are recorded for Spain; how far they reach this area is not established here.
Under Franco's State.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Autonomous Community of the Canary Islands
eras.note: Under the Constitution of 1978. The autonomous community dates from 1982: the date is given as 16 August 1982 or 10 August 1983 depending on the source.

regions.label: Madrid and its province
regions.sub: Madrid, El Escorial, San Agustín del Guadalix

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — the Spanish monarchy
eras.note: Parish registers run from the Council of Trent (FamilySearch gives 1545 and 1563); most registers over 100 years old were moved to the archive of the parish's diocese. Madrid's territory belonged to the archdiocese of Toledo, so look in Toledo's records too.

eras.polity: Spain under Joseph Bonaparte — Peninsular War
eras.note: Joseph Bonaparte's reign is dated from June or August 1808 depending on the source, to 11 December 1813; the Peninsular War ended on 17 April 1814. An 1810 Napoleonic division of Spain into 84 prefectures is recorded.
The war ended on 17 April 1814 and the Bourbon monarchy was restored; the 1822 division of Spain into provinces, made in the Trienio Liberal, was the predecessor of the 1833 one.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Province of Madrid
eras.note: Madrid became a province by the royal decree of 30 November 1833, in Castilla la Nueva.

Civil registration is dated from 1871 (FamilySearch's church-records page says 1869), with some municipalities holding records from as early as 1837; the records are still in each municipality's archive, and certificates are requested through the Ministerio de Justicia. The diocese of Madrid-Alcalá, split from Toledo, dates from 1884 or 1885 depending on the source.

eras.polity: Second Republic — Madrid in the Republican zone
eras.note: Madrid stayed with the Republic after the July 1936 coup, with the Guadarrama front to its north holding until 1939; Casado's coup began on 5 March 1939 and Nationalist troops entered Madrid without further fighting on 28 March. FamilySearch notes record loss in the Civil War without listing registers. An inventory of one archdiocese (Valencia) put the gap mostly before 1871, so check each parish's diocesan archive.

eras.polity: Spain — Franco's State, then the transition to the 1978 Constitution
eras.note: Franco announced the end of the war on 1 April 1939, days after Madrid fell.
On 23 July 1991 the archdiocese of Madrid ceded territory to create the dioceses of Alcalá de Henares and Getafe, so a parish in the province may now answer to any of the three.

regions.label: La Mancha — Ciudad Real
regions.sub: Almagro, Valdepeñas, Herencia

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — Toledo and the military orders
eras.note: The territory belonged partly to the archdiocese of Toledo, to a lesser extent to the diocese of Córdoba, and in zones governed by the military orders: Santiago through the priorato nullius of Uclés (in Cuenca), Calatrava through the priorato nullius of Almagro. Which applies to a given town is not established here. Parish registers run from the Council of Trent (FamilySearch gives 1545 and 1563); most registers over 100 years old were moved to the archive of the parish's diocese.

eras.polity: Spain under Joseph Bonaparte — Peninsular War
eras.note: Joseph Bonaparte's reign is dated from June or August 1808 depending on the source, to 11 December 1813; the Peninsular War ended on 17 April 1814. An 1810 Napoleonic division of Spain into 84 prefectures is recorded.
The war ended on 17 April 1814 and the Bourbon monarchy was restored; the 1822 division of Spain into provinces, made in the Trienio Liberal, was the predecessor of the 1833 one.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Province of Ciudad Real
eras.note: Ciudad Real became a province by the royal decree of 30 November 1833, in Castilla la Nueva; the 1851 concordat planned a diocese of Ciudad Real but no bull was issued. Civil registration is dated from 1871 (FamilySearch's church-records page says 1869), with some municipalities holding records from as early as 1837; the records are still in each municipality's archive, and certificates are requested through the Ministerio de Justicia.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — the Priorato of the Military Orders at Ciudad Real
eras.note: The Republic suppressed the military orders on 9 March 1873, and the bull Quo gravius of 14 July 1873 suppressed their jurisdiction and shared their territories among neighbouring dioceses. The bull Ad Apostolicam of 18 November 1875 set up the priorato nullius of the Military Orders, put into effect on 15 May 1876 and promulgated at Ciudad Real on 4 June 1876; for a parish inside its territory the Priorato, not Toledo, is the church authority to ask.

The Republic kept the central area around Madrid after the July 1936 coup; the last Republican territory was occupied in the final days of March 1939, and the date for Ciudad Real itself is not established here. FamilySearch notes record loss in the Civil War without listing registers. An inventory of one archdiocese (Valencia) put the gap mostly before 1871, so check each parish's diocesan archive.

eras.polity: Spain — Franco's State, then the transition to the 1978 Constitution
eras.note: Franco announced the end of the war on 1 April 1939.
The Priorato became the diocese of Ciudad Real, a suffragan of Toledo, on 4 February 1980 (bull Episcopus titulo Doritanus); its bishop remained prior of the Orders.

regions.label: Old Castile and La Rioja
regions.sub: Burgos, Segovia, Soria, La Granja, Santo Domingo de Silos, Logroño

eras.note: Parish registers run from the Council of Trent (FamilySearch gives 1545 and 1563); most registers over 100 years old were moved to the archive of the parish's diocese. La Rioja's parishes belong to the diocese of Calahorra y La Calzada, whose territory once also took in Álava, Vizcaya and parts of Navarre, Guipúzcoa, Burgos and Soria.

eras.polity: Spain under Joseph Bonaparte — Peninsular War
eras.note: Joseph Bonaparte's reign is dated from June or August 1808 depending on the source, to 11 December 1813; the Peninsular War ended on 17 April 1814. An 1810 Napoleonic division of Spain into 84 prefectures is recorded.
The war ended on 17 April 1814 and the Bourbon monarchy was restored; the 1822 division of Spain into provinces, made in the Trienio Liberal, was the predecessor of the 1833 one.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — provinces of Castilla la Vieja
eras.note: The royal decree of 30 November 1833 made Burgos, Logroño, Segovia and Soria provinces of Castilla la Vieja, with Ávila, Palencia, Santander and Valladolid.

Civil registration is dated from 1871 (FamilySearch's church-records page says 1869), with some municipalities holding records from as early as 1837; the records are still in each municipality's archive, and certificates are requested through the Ministerio de Justicia.

The Second Republic ran from 1931 to the July 1936 coup, when Old Castile and León, described as conservative and Catholic areas, fell quickly to the rebels; conspirators took the command posts in Burgos on 19 July.

Nationalist forces secured the Somosierra and Alto del León passes by 25 July 1936 and the Guadarrama front then held until 1939; La Rioja and Álava are described as Nationalist-leaning areas. FamilySearch notes record loss in the Civil War without listing registers.

eras.polity: Spain — Franco's State, then the transition to the 1978 Constitution
eras.note: In 1949 the Condado de Treviño went to Vitoria. Decrees of 2 September and 22 November 1955 adjusted Calahorra to the civil province of La Rioja: Viana and Amescoas went to Pamplona, Yanguas and San Pedro Manrique to Osma, ten parishes to Burgos, and Alfaro, Canales, Ezcaray and Treviana came in; 'Logroño' was added to the diocese's name on 9 March 1959.
The diocese of Calahorra y La Calzada-Logroño now coincides with the autonomous community of La Rioja.

regions.label: The Cantabrian coast — Asturias and Cantabria
regions.sub: Llanes, Santander, the Cantabrian coast

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — Burgos and Oviedo dioceses
eras.note: Parish registers run from the Council of Trent (FamilySearch gives 1545 and 1563); most registers over 100 years old were moved to the archive of the parish's diocese. The Santander coast then belonged to the archdiocese of Burgos, with part of it from the diocese of Oviedo.

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — new diocese of Santander
eras.note: The diocese of Santander was erected on 12 December 1754 by the bull Romanus Pontifex, out of Burgos and Oviedo, and runs from the Cantabrian range to the sea; parishes in it answer to Santander from then.

eras.polity: Spain under Joseph Bonaparte — Peninsular War
eras.note: Joseph Bonaparte's reign is dated from June or August 1808 depending on the source, to 11 December 1813; the Peninsular War ended on 17 April 1814. An 1810 Napoleonic division of Spain into 84 prefectures is recorded.
The war ended on 17 April 1814 and the Bourbon monarchy was restored; the 1822 division of Spain into provinces, made in the Trienio Liberal, was the predecessor of the 1833 one.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — provinces of Oviedo and Santander
eras.note: The royal decree of 30 November 1833 created the province of Oviedo and the province of Santander, the latter among the provinces of Castilla la Vieja.

Civil registration is dated from 1871 (FamilySearch's church-records page says 1869), with some municipalities holding records from as early as 1837; the records are still in each municipality's archive, and certificates are requested through the Ministerio de Justicia.

eras.polity: Second Republic — the northern Republican enclave
eras.note: After the July 1936 coup the Republic retained control of Cantabria and most of Asturias, which with Biscay formed a Republican enclave. The Nationalist offensive on Cantabria began on 14 August 1937 and the Italians occupied Santander on 26 August; the Nationalists occupied Gijón by 21 October 1937, ending the war in the north.

eras.polity: Spain — Franco's State, then the transition to the 1978 Constitution
eras.note: This ground came under Franco's government in 1937, two years before the rest of the Republican zone. FamilySearch notes record loss in the Civil War without listing registers.
The province of Oviedo was renamed Asturias in 1983.

regions.label: The Basque provinces — Álava, Bizkaia, Gipuzkoa
regions.sub: Bilbao, San Sebastián, Vitoria-Gasteiz

eras.polity: Álava, Biscay and Gipuzkoa under their own fueros
eras.note: Parish registers run from the Council of Trent (FamilySearch gives 1545 and 1563); most registers over 100 years old were moved to the archive of the parish's diocese. Until 1861 their parishes were split among the dioceses of Calahorra, Burgos, Pamplona and Santander, so one province's registers can lie in several diocesan archives. The three provinces had their own fueros, partly suppressed in 1839 and totally in 1876.

eras.polity: Spain under Joseph Bonaparte — Peninsular War
eras.note: Joseph Bonaparte's reign is dated from June or August 1808 depending on the source, to 11 December 1813; the Peninsular War ended on 17 April 1814. An 1810 Napoleonic division of Spain into 84 prefectures is recorded.

The three provinces kept their historic names in the 1833 division. The First Carlist War (1833-1840) was fought mainly in the Basque Country and elsewhere, and the Convention of Bergara of 1839 partly suppressed their self-government.

The diocese of Vitoria was erected on 8 September 1861 (its first bishop took possession in 1862) from parts of Burgos, Calahorra, Pamplona and Santander. The Third Carlist War ran 1872-1876. Civil registration is dated from 1871 (FamilySearch's church-records page says 1869), with some municipalities holding records from as early as 1837; the records are still in each municipality's archive, and certificates are requested through the Ministerio de Justicia.

The law of 21 July 1876 ended the fueros and made the provinces pay taxes like other Spaniards; the royal decree of 28 February 1878 set up the Concierto Económico under which provincial councils collect taxes and pay a fixed quota to the State.
A Basque statute failed in 1932.

eras.polity: Civil War — Álava Nationalist; Biscay and Gipuzkoa Republican at first
eras.note: In July 1936 Vitoria in Álava was easily seized by the rebels, while the rising failed in Biscay and Gipuzkoa. Gipuzkoa was Republican until Irun and San Sebastián fell in September 1936, and the Nationalists entered Bilbao on 19 June 1937. The Statute of Autonomy of October 1936 was enforced only in Biscay and was abolished automatically when Nationalist troops occupied the territory.

eras.polity: Spain — Franco's State, then the transition to the 1978 Constitution
eras.note: A decree-law of 23 June 1937 abolished the Concierto Económico for Biscay and Gipuzkoa, which it branded traitor provinces; Álava kept its agreement. On 2 November 1949 the dioceses of Bilbao and San Sebastián were separated from Vitoria.

The 1978 Constitution restored the suspended prerogatives; the Statute of Gernika was approved by referendum on 25 October 1979 and Law 12/1981 approved the Concierto Económico for the whole Basque Country.

regions.label: Navarre
regions.sub: Pamplona, Estella, Tudela

eras.polity: Kingdom of Navarre within the Crown of Castile
eras.note: Ferdinand's forces invaded in 1512 and Navarre south of the Pyrenees was annexed to the Crown of Castile in 1515, keeping a separate and ambiguous status and home rule. Parish registers run from the Council of Trent (FamilySearch gives 1545 and 1563); most registers over 100 years old were moved to the archive of the parish's diocese.

eras.polity: Spain under Joseph Bonaparte — Peninsular War
