Russia's Fort Ross in northern California was established in 1812 and sold in 1841. U.S. forces took the northern ports in 1846, Californios surrendered in the Treaty of Cahuenga on January 13, 1847, and Mexico ceded California in 1848.

eras.polity: United States — ceded California, not yet a state
eras.note: The Gold Rush began in 1848. California was admitted as a state on September 9, 1850 with no territorial period.
Statewide registration of births and deaths began in 1905. Earlier events are in the county recorder's records, and some counties kept records from the mid-1800s.

regions.label: Nevada — Great Basin to the Comstock
regions.sub: Reno, Carson City, Virginia City, Las Vegas, Elko

eras.polity: Claimed as part of Spanish Alta California
eras.note: Before registers. Present-day Nevada lay within the territory of Alta California; the Franciscan Francisco Garcés was the first European to enter the area, in the 1770s.
Mexican Alta California included present-day Nevada. Jedediah Smith entered the Las Vegas Valley in 1827.
Utah Territory, organised on September 9, 1850, covered most of present-day Nevada. Mormon way stations from 1851 began a permanent American presence, and the Comstock Lode was discovered in 1859.
Congress created Nevada Territory on March 2, 1861.

Nevada was admitted on October 31, 1864; its eastern and southern boundaries were enlarged in 1866-67, so places in the east and south were earlier in other territories. The state holds birth and death records from July 1, 1911, and earlier records are generally with the county recorder.

regions.label: Utah — Mexican ground to Deseret and Utah Territory
regions.sub: Salt Lake City, Ogden, Provo, St. George, Logan

eras.polity: Claimed as part of Spanish Alta California
eras.note: Before registers. The Spanish province of Alta California was described as including all of present-day Utah.
Utah lay within Mexican Alta California until the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 1848. The Mormon pioneers entered the Salt Lake Valley on July 24, 1847, when the land still belonged to Mexico.

eras.polity: State of Deseret (provisional) in ceded territory
eras.note: The Mormon settlers formed the provisional State of Deseret, dated to March 12, 1849 in one study; it served as the de facto government before Congress acted. Sources differ on when Deseret ended (1850 or 1851).

Congress organised Utah Territory on September 9, 1850; it then covered present Utah, most of Nevada, western Colorado and a corner of Wyoming, and lost ground when Nevada Territory and Colorado Territory were formed in 1861 and Wyoming Territory in 1868. Fillmore was the capital to 1856, then Salt Lake City. A Church History Library database names the pioneers who came to Utah from 1847 to 1868.

Utah became the 45th state on January 4, 1896. Statewide birth and death registration began in 1905, with county clerks keeping registers from 1898; the Utah State Archives holds the permanent records.

regions.label: Colorado — from Kansas, Nebraska, Utah and New Mexico territories
regions.sub: Denver, Pueblo, Colorado Springs, Durango, San Luis

eras.polity: Spanish claim south and west of the Arkansas River
eras.note: Before registers. Juan Bautista de Anza founded San Carlos near present-day Pueblo in 1787, and the settlement quickly failed.
The Treaty of Córdoba gave Mexico Spain's territorial claims in 1821. The Arkansas River line was set by the Adams-Onís Treaty of 1819: U.S. claims south and west of the river were ceded to Spain.

eras.polity: Kansas, Nebraska, Utah and New Mexico territories
eras.note: Before February 28, 1861 a Colorado place lay in Kansas, Nebraska, Utah or New Mexico territory, so earlier county and probate records are filed under those. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) opened the southern Rockies to American settlement, the Pikes Peak Gold Rush began in July 1858, and the extralegal Jefferson Territory existed from October 24, 1859 to 1861. In the Compromise of 1850 Texas gave up claims to land including parts of present-day Colorado.

Congress organised Colorado Territory on February 28, 1861 and the legislature created 17 counties on November 1, 1861. The Sand Creek Massacre took place in November 1864 during the Colorado War of 1863-65.
Colorado became the 38th state on August 1, 1876. Statewide birth and death registration began in 1907, though some counties began as early as 1876; the Colorado State Archives is in Denver.

regions.label: Montana and Wyoming — Louisiana Purchase and Oregon Country to territories
regions.sub: Billings, Helena, Missoula, Cheyenne, Casper, Laramie

eras.polity: Louisiana Purchase east of the Continental Divide; Oregon Country west of it
eras.note: Wyoming's ground east of the Continental Divide and Montana's east of it were part of the 1803 Louisiana Purchase; ground west of the Divide and north of the 42nd parallel was in the Oregon Country, where Britain and the United States shared access from 1818 until the Oregon Treaty of June 15, 1846. A corner of southwestern Wyoming came to the U.S. in the Mexican Cession of 1848.

eras.polity: Oregon, Washington, Nebraska, Dakota and Utah territories
eras.note: Ground west of the Divide lay in Oregon Territory (1848), then Washington Territory (1853); ground east of it lay in Nebraska Territory and from March 2, 1861 in Dakota Territory, which then included much of present Montana and Wyoming. Records before 1863 therefore sit under those territories.

eras.polity: Idaho Territory, Montana Territory and Dakota Territory
eras.note: Idaho Territory was created on March 3 or 4, 1863 (dated differently by source) out of land that included Dakota's. Montana Territory was organised from Idaho Territory on May 26, 1864 (dated May 28 in one account), and Wyoming Territory followed on July 25, 1868, formed from Dakota, Idaho and Utah territories.

Wyoming's territorial government was organised on April 17, 1869, and in 1872 the territory had five counties: Albany, Carbon, Laramie, Sweetwater and Uinta. Montana became a state on November 8, 1889, and Wyoming on July 10, 1890.

Statewide birth and death registration began in Montana in 1907 (practitioners were first required to keep records in 1895) and in Wyoming in 1909, with some earlier county registers in Albany and Laramie counties.

regions.label: Oregon — Oregon Country, Provisional Government, Territory and State
regions.sub: Portland, Salem, Eugene, Oregon City, Astoria, Pendleton, Medford

eras.polity: Oregon Country — joint British and American occupation
eras.note: An 1818 arrangement gave Britain and the United States shared access to the region. The Hudson's Bay Company had almost complete control after its 1821 merger with the North West Company and made Fort Vancouver its headquarters from 1825.

eras.polity: Oregon Country — joint occupation, settlers' Provisional Government
eras.note: The Provisional Government of Oregon ran from 1843 to 1849, during the last years of joint occupation.

eras.polity: Oregon Treaty — Provisional Government of Oregon
eras.note: The Oregon Treaty of June 15, 1846 settled the boundary with Britain, with the Oregon Country divided along the 49th parallel. The Provisional Government continued until 1849.

Congress created Oregon Territory in 1848 (14 August 1848; some sources give 1846). It covered present Idaho, Oregon and Washington and the parts of Montana and Wyoming west of the Continental Divide until Washington Territory was split off on March 2, 1853. The Donation Land Claim Act dates from 1850.

Oregon was admitted as a state on February 14, 1859 within its present boundaries. Statewide birth and death registration began under a 1903 law, though some counties began registering as early as 1845.

regions.label: Washington and Idaho — Oregon Country to territories and statehood
regions.sub: Seattle, Olympia, Spokane, Walla Walla, Vancouver WA, Boise, Lewiston

eras.polity: Oregon Country — joint British and American occupation
eras.note: An 1818 arrangement gave Britain and the United States shared access to the region. The Hudson's Bay Company had almost complete control after its 1821 merger with the North West Company and made Fort Vancouver its headquarters from 1825.

eras.polity: Oregon Treaty — Provisional Government of Oregon
eras.note: The Oregon Treaty of June 15, 1846 settled the boundary with Britain, with the Oregon Country divided along the 49th parallel. The Provisional Government of Oregon continued until 1849.

Congress created Oregon Territory in 1848 (14 August 1848; some sources give 1846). It covered present Idaho, Oregon and Washington and the parts of Montana and Wyoming west of the Continental Divide.
Washington Territory was created on March 2, 1853 and at its largest included all of present Idaho.
Idaho Territory was created on March 3 or 4, 1863 (dated differently by source), which gave Washington Territory its present boundaries.

eras.polity: United States — State of Washington and State of Idaho
eras.note: Washington became a state on November 11, 1889; Idaho followed on July 3, 1890, so Idaho records of 1889-90 are still territorial. Statewide death registration began in Washington in 1907 and in Idaho in 1911 (county-level registration is sometimes dated 1907 for Idaho).

regions.label: Alaska — Russian America to statehood
regions.sub: Sitka, Juneau, Kodiak, Anchorage, Fairbanks, Nome, the Aleutians

eras.note: Russia's first permanent Alaskan settlement was founded at Three Saints Bay, Kodiak, in 1784; the Russian-American Company was chartered in 1799 and New Archangel (Sitka) became the capital in 1808. The Russian Orthodox Church kept the parish registers: the Diocese of Alaska archives were deposited in the Library of Congress (by 1927 or 1940 depending on the source), with microfilm at the National Archives Pacific Alaska Region and the Alaska State Library, and FamilySearch has Alaska Russian Orthodox records for 1845-1917.
The United States bought Alaska in 1867 for $7.2 million and the formal transfer is dated October 18, 1867. Control passed among the Army, Treasury and Navy before civil administration began.
Alaska was reorganised as the District of Alaska in 1884. Gold in Canada's Yukon in 1896 and at Nome in 1899 brought gold-rush traffic through the district.

The Second Organic Act of 1912 made it the Territory of Alaska. In the Aleutian campaign of 1942-43 Japanese forces occupied Attu and Kiska; Aleut residents were evacuated or interned and the Attuans were resettled at Atka after the war.
Alaska was admitted as a state on January 3, 1959.

regions.label: Hawaii — Kingdom, Republic, Territory and State
regions.sub: Honolulu, Hilo, Lahaina, Kauai, Maui, Molokai

eras.note: Kamehameha I established the kingdom in 1795 and Kauai and Niihau joined in 1810, so the unification is dated 1795 or 1810 depending on the source. The monarchy was absolute until the constitution of 1840.

The Great Mahele of 1848 divided the land; each claim was either awarded a Land Commission Award or not, and the awards often name parents, siblings and spouses. The Hawaii State Archives holds marriage records from 1826 and birth and death records from 1853, which are incomplete before 1896.

eras.polity: Overthrow of the monarchy and the Republic of Hawaii
eras.note: The monarchy was overthrown on January 17, 1893 by the Committee of Safety, backed by U.S. forces. The Republic of Hawaii was established in 1894 and lasted until 1898.

The Newlands Resolution was signed on July 7, 1898 and annexation took effect on August 12, 1898. The Hawaiian Organic Act of April 30, 1900 organised the Territory, and martial law was in force from 1941 to 1944.
Hawaii was admitted as the 50th state on August 21, 1959.

regions.label: Valley of Mexico and the central highlands
regions.sub: Mexico City, Toluca, Cuernavaca, Pachuca, Puebla, Tlaxcala

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Kingdom of New Spain — viceroyalty from 1535
eras.note: Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521 and the city was rebuilt as Ciudad de México. The Audiencia of Mexico dates from 1527 and the viceroyalty from a decree of 12 October 1535, with Antonio de Mendoza as first viceroy. Parish books come from the dioceses (Tlaxcala is dated 1527, Mexico City 1530), with a copy kept in the diocesan archive; Cortés held the Marquesado del Valle, about 4,000 km² around Cuernavaca, from his title of 1529.

eras.polity: Viceroyalty of New Spain — intendancies of México and Puebla
eras.note: Intendancies were created on the mainland from 1786, including México and Puebla de los Ángeles (Puebla is dated 1786 or 1787 depending on the passage). The Marquis's lands were confiscated in 1809. The declaration of independence is dated 27 or 28 September 1821.

eras.polity: First Mexican Empire, then the federal republic
eras.note: The empire lasted from independence in 1821 to Iturbide's abdication on 19 March 1823. The territory around the capital was organised as the Federal District on 18 November 1824; the rest stayed in the State of Mexico, whose capital moved to Texcoco and later Toluca.
The federal constitution was repealed on 23 October 1835 and the states became departments under the central government, until the 1824 constitution was restored on 22 August 1846.
Civil registration was established on 28 July 1859 and records are held at municipio level, with the Federal District keeping its own in delegations. It was not vigorously enforced until 1867.

Maximilian accepted the crown on 10 April 1864 and reached the capital on 12 June 1864; French forces held central Mexico including Mexico City during the empire, which ended with his execution on 19 June 1867.

eras.polity: Restored Republic — Federal District, then Ciudad de México
eras.note: Hidalgo (16 January 1869) was cut from the State of Mexico out of the districts of Tula, Tulancingo and Huejutla, and Morelos (17 April 1869) from the same state, so earlier events at Pachuca, Tulancingo or Cuernavaca are in the State of Mexico's papers. The Federal District was renamed Ciudad de México on 29 January 2016.

regions.label: Gulf lowlands — Veracruz and Tabasco
regions.sub: Veracruz, Xalapa, Orizaba, Villahermosa, Coatzacoalcos, Tuxpan

eras.polity: New Spain — Veracruz, the port of the viceroyalty; Tabasco
eras.note: Cortés founded Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz on 18 May 1519, the first Spanish town in what is now Mexico, and fought the Battle of Centla in Tabasco the same year. Santa María de la Victoria in Tabasco was sacked by pirates and the town moved inland in 1598 to San Juan Bautista, later Villahermosa. Gaspar Yanga's rebellion ran 1609-1618 and a 1618 amnesty let Africans form their own community, later the municipality of Yanga.

eras.polity: Intendancy of Veracruz — Free Commerce decree of 1778
eras.note: Veracruz was made an intendancy in 1786 (1787 in another passage of the same source), after the Decree of Free Commerce of 1778 raised the port's trade.

eras.polity: Mexico — states of Veracruz and Tabasco
eras.note: Spanish troops held the fort of San Juan de Ulúa until 1823. Veracruz was admitted as a state on 22 December 1823 and Tabasco was one of the first fourteen states of the 1824 constitution. French forces blockaded and bombarded Veracruz in 1838 (the Pastry War).

eras.polity: Reform, French intervention and Second Empire
eras.note: Spanish, British and French forces occupied Veracruz in late 1861; the French stayed on to install Maximilian and were expelled through the port in 1866-1867. National civil registration dates from 28 July 1859.
United States troops occupied Veracruz for six months from April 1914 after the Tampico Affair.

regions.label: Oaxaca
regions.sub: Oaxaca, Tehuantepec, Salina Cruz, Tuxtepec, Huatulco, Pinotepa Nacional

eras.polity: New Spain — Oaxaca and the Marquesado del Valle
eras.note: Cortés's captains reached Oaxaca shortly after the fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521, Dominicans settled in the city in 1528 and the bishopric was formed in 1535. Cortés was named Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca in 1529. Parish books follow the diocese, and a copy of each went to the diocesan archive.
Oaxaca appears among the intendancies created in 1786.

Oaxaca is dated as a state from 21 December 1823 or 1824 depending on the source, with José María Murguía its first governor. In 1842 Oaxacan forces under Santa Anna occupied Soconusco, then disputed between Chiapas and Guatemala.
Civil registration began nationally on 28 July 1859. French forces held cities as far south as Oaxaca during the Second Empire.
Oaxaca archives its civil registration records at district level rather than by municipio, as Guerrero does.

regions.label: Chiapas and Soconusco
regions.sub: Tuxtla Gutiérrez, San Cristóbal de las Casas, Comitán, Tapachula, Palenque

eras.polity: Governed from Guatemala, not Mexico City
eras.note: Cortés sent tax collectors in 1522, Luis Marín led the first military incursion in 1523 and San Cristóbal was founded in 1528 (as Ciudad Real, renamed in 1828). Chiapas, Soconusco and Tuxtla were under the regional colonial government of Guatemala.

eras.polity: Intendancy of Chiapas, within Guatemala's jurisdiction
eras.note: The Bourbon reforms united the three regions as the intendancy of Chiapas in 1790, though the Chiapas-Soconusco division stayed strong.

Several towns, beginning with Comitán, declared separation from Spain in 1821, Iturbide decreed Chiapas part of Mexico in 1822, and in 1823 a Junta General declared independence again. In July 1824 Soconusco split from Chiapas and announced it would join the Central American Federation, and a September 1824 referendum on joining Central America or Mexico favoured Mexico.

The State of Chiapas was declared in 1824 and adopted its first constitution in 1826. Soconusco stayed neutral from 1824 to 1842, when forces under Santa Anna occupied it; its elites accepted reincorporation in 1844.
The Chiapas-Guatemala border was agreed in 1882 and Guatemala formally recognised the annexation of Soconusco in 1895. Civil registration dates from 28 July 1859 and is held by municipio.

regions.label: Yucatán Peninsula
regions.sub: Mérida, Campeche, Chetumal, Cancún, Valladolid, Progreso

eras.note: Montejo reached Cozumel in late September 1527, Campeche was founded in 1540, Mérida on 6 January 1542, and the conquest ended in 1544 with the founding of Salamanca de Bacalar.
The Captaincy General, created in 1617, gave the province more autonomy within New Spain. Pirates attacked Campeche repeatedly, Laurens de Graaf sacked it in 1685, and a wall was built afterwards.
An intendancy covering the same area is dated 1786 in one source and 1789 in another.

eras.polity: Yucatán in the Mexican Empire and federation
eras.note: Yucatán declared independence from Spain at Mérida on 15 September 1821 and joined the Mexican Empire on 2 November 1821. A first Republic of Yucatán is dated 29 May 1823, and it entered the federation on 23 December 1823.

eras.polity: Republic of Yucatán — independent of Mexico 1841-43 and from 1846
eras.note: Independence was proclaimed on 16 March 1841, a Mexican general withdrew by sea on 24 April 1843 and autonomy was granted on 5 December 1843. Yucatán declared independence again on 1 January 1846 and the Caste War began at Tepich on 30 July 1847. The Republic was disestablished on 14 July 1848, with the return to the Mexican confederation ordered on 17 August 1848.

Campeche separated from Yucatán on 3 May 1858, was a federal territory until 29 April 1863, and then became a state. In the south-east the Caste War produced an independent Maya state centred on Chan Santa Cruz (now Felipe Carrillo Puerto), which kept considerable independence for decades; national civil registration dates from 28 July 1859.

Quintana Roo was created as a federal territory by decree on 24 November 1902, was declared part of Yucatán again in 1913 and a separate territory again in 1915, and became a state on 8 October 1974. The area was long part of Yucatán.

regions.label: Baja California peninsula
regions.sub: Tijuana, Mexicali, Ensenada, La Paz, Loreto, Cabo San Lucas

eras.note: The Jesuits founded their permanent mission at Loreto in 1697 and later Santa Gertrudis, San Borja and Santa María (1752-1767).
The Jesuits were expelled in 1768; Franciscans administered the missions until 1773, when Dominicans took over and founded missions from El Rosario (1774) to Descanso (1817).
In 1804 Spain divided California into Alta and Baja California along the line between the Franciscan and Dominican missions.

Mexico ordered the missions secularised in 1833. By the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (2 February 1848) the United States took Alta California while Mexico kept Baja California including the sites of Tijuana, Mexicali and Tecate. William Walker seized La Paz in 1853 and declared a Republic of Baja California; Mexican forces expelled him after several months.
Civil registration began nationally on 28 July 1859. The Magonista movement started in 1905, and Mexicali and Tijuana were briefly captured in 1911 before surrendering to federal forces.

eras.polity: Northern and Southern territories — Baja California state from 1952
eras.note: The territory was split into Northern and Southern territories in 1931, and the Northern Territory became the state of Baja California in 1952.

eras.polity: Baja California and Baja California Sur
eras.note: The Southern Territory became the state of Baja California Sur in 1974; Loreto lies in it, while Tijuana, Mexicali and Tecate are in Baja California.

regions.label: Sonora and Sinaloa
regions.sub: Hermosillo, Álamos, Culiacán, Mazatlán, Guaymas, Ciudad Obregón

eras.polity: Jesuit missions of Sinaloa and Sonora — Nueva Navarra, then Sonora
eras.note: Jesuits began working in the coastal lowlands in the 1610s. The province was called Nueva Navarra in 1637 and renamed Sonora in 1648, and Eusebio Kino founded missions in the Pimería Alta from 1687, starting at Cucurpe.

eras.polity: Provincias de Sonora, Ostimuri y Sinaloa
eras.note: Sonora and Sinaloa were joined as one province in 1691, a union that lasted until 1823. The Yaqui and Mayo uprisings came in 1740-1742 and the Jesuits were expelled in 1767, ending the mission system.
Sonora is on the list of intendancies created in 1786.

The two provinces were one state from 1824, with its constitution adopted on 31 October 1825 under the name Estado de Occidente, and capitals at El Fuerte, Cosalá and Álamos. It was divided into Sonora and Sinaloa on 30 September 1830; another source dates the division to 1823-1824.

eras.polity: Separate states of Sonora and Sinaloa
eras.note: Sonora's first state constitution came in 1831, with the capital moved to Hermosillo. In the Gadsden Purchase of 1853 Sonora lost more than 29,000 square miles, mostly land now in southern Arizona.
Civil registration dates from 28 July 1859. Yaqui resistance in Sonora led to uprisings and forced deportations between 1887 and 1908, peaking in 1904-1908.

regions.label: Chihuahua (Nueva Vizcaya, north)
regions.sub: Chihuahua, Ciudad Juárez, Parral, Casas Grandes, Ojinaga

eras.polity: Nueva Vizcaya, New Spain — capital at Durango
eras.note: Francisco de Ibarra established Nueva Vizcaya in 1562, covering most of present Chihuahua and Durango with its capital at Durango. The diocese of Durango is dated 1620.

The Commandancy General of the Internal Provinces dates from 1776 or 1777 depending on the source. The intendancy at Durango is dated 1786 or 1787, and the Internal Provinces were split into eastern and western commandancies in 1788, restored in 1813 and lasted to 1821.

eras.polity: Nueva Vizcaya succeeded by Chihuahua and Durango
eras.note: Independence on 27 September 1821 ended Nueva Vizcaya, which Chihuahua and Durango succeeded. Congress decreed the division on 19 July 1823 and gave the city of Chihuahua the title of city.

The separation of Chihuahua and Durango was affirmed on 22 May and 6 July 1824 and both states issued constitutions in 1825. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 2 February 1848 set the Rio Grande boundary to the south edge of New Mexico.
Civil registration dates from 28 July 1859, kept by municipio.

regions.label: Durango
regions.sub: Durango, Gómez Palacio, Santiago Papasquiaro, Mapimí, El Salto

eras.note: Nueva Vizcaya was established in 1562 with its capital at Durango; Spanish exploration of Nueva Vizcaya began in 1531 with Nuño de Guzmán's expedition. The diocese of Durango is dated 1620, and its parish records are indexed through New Mexico State University.

The Durango intendancy is listed under 1786 in one source and 1787 in another. In July-September 1821 royalist General José de la Cruz held Durango against Negrete's forces until a truce on 3 September.

eras.polity: Nueva Vizcaya succeeded by Durango and Chihuahua
eras.note: Durango's troops and people declared against Emperor Iturbide on 5 March 1823, and Congress decreed Durango's separation from Chihuahua on 19 July 1823.
The separation was affirmed in 1824 and Durango issued its constitution in 1825.
Civil registration began on 28 July 1859 and is kept at municipio level.

regions.label: North-east — Coahuila, Nuevo León, Tamaulipas
regions.sub: Monterrey, Saltillo, Reynosa, Matamoros, Tampico, Piedras Negras

eras.polity: Nuevo Reino de León, Coahuila and Nueva Vizcaya
eras.note: The first Spanish settlement in Coahuila was Minas de la Trinidad in 1577. Philip II authorised the Nuevo Reyno de León in 1582, with Luis de Carabajal as its first governor, and Saltillo was settled in 1586 as part of Nueva Vizcaya.
José de Escandón founded Nuevo Santander in 1747 (some sources say 1746), covering today's Tamaulipas and extending into southern Texas; Jiménez, founded in 1755, was its capital.

Nuevo León and Nuevo Santander were placed under the Provincias Internas in 1776; when the commandancy was split in 1786 (1788 in another source) they, with Coahuila and Texas, formed the Eastern Internal Provinces. Nuevo Santander was renamed Tamaulipas after independence.

eras.polity: Mexico — Coahuila y Tejas, Nuevo León, Tamaulipas
eras.note: Under the 1824 constitution Coahuila was joined with Texas as Coahuila y Tejas, with Monclova as capital from 1833 to 1835, until Texas seceded in 1836.

eras.polity: Mexico — northern frontier contested with Texas
eras.note: The strip between the Nueces and the Rio Grande was claimed by Texas but administered by Mexico. A provisional junta of the northern frontier, called the Republic of the Rio Grande, ran from 23 January to 6 November 1840 and met at Guerrero, Tamaulipas.

The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (2 February 1848) made the Rio Grande the boundary, and residents of ceded land had one year to choose citizenship. Santiago Vidaurri annexed Coahuila to Nuevo León on 19 February 1856, and French forces held cities as far north as Monterrey. Civil registration began nationally on 28 July 1859.

eras.polity: Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas as separate states
eras.note: Coahuila's separation from Nuevo León is dated 1868.

regions.label: Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí and Aguascalientes
regions.sub: Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí, Fresnillo, Aguascalientes, Real de Catorce

eras.note: Juan de Tolosa founded Zacatecas in 1546 after a rich silver find. Los Zacatecas was one of the provinces of the Kingdom of Nueva Galicia, whose Audiencia sat at Guadalajara from 1548 and became independent of Mexico City's in 1572.

eras.polity: Nueva Galicia and New Spain — mining provinces
eras.note: The town of San Luis Potosí is traditionally dated to 1592, after gold and silver finds.

eras.polity: Intendancies of Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí
eras.note: Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí both appear among the intendancies created in 1786.

eras.polity: Mexico — states of Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí
eras.note: San Luis Potosí was admitted as a state on 22 December 1823 and Zacatecas on 23 December 1823, with a state constitution for San Luis Potosí on 16 October 1826.

eras.polity: Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí and Aguascalientes
eras.note: Civil registration dates from 28 July 1859, kept by municipio.

regions.label: Nueva Galicia — Jalisco, Nayarit and Colima
regions.sub: Guadalajara, Puerto Vallarta, Tepic, Colima, Manzanillo, Lagos de Moreno

eras.polity: Kingdom of Nueva Galicia — Guzmán's conquest
eras.note: Nuño de Guzmán's expedition began in 1531 and the kingdom's capital moved from Compostela (1531-1540) to Tepic (1540-1560) before Guadalajara. The Mixtón War ran 1540-1541.

Guadalajara became the seat of a second mainland Audiencia in 1548 and was independent of the Mexico City Audiencia from 1572. The Guadalajara diocese is dated 1548 and the last independent Cora communities were taken into Spanish administration by force in 1722.
Guadalajara is among the intendancies created in 1786.

eras.polity: State of Jalisco and Territory of Colima
eras.note: After independence Nueva Galicia became the State of Jalisco and the Territory of Colima in 1824.

eras.polity: Jalisco — Nayarit still part of it
eras.note: Civil registration dates from 28 July 1859.
Nayarit became a state in 1917, dated 26 January or 1 May depending on the passage.

regions.label: The Bajío — Guanajuato and Querétaro
regions.sub: Guanajuato, León, San Miguel de Allende, Querétaro, Celaya, Irapuato

eras.polity: New Spain — silver and agriculture of the Bajío
eras.note: Cristóbal de Olid's expedition reached the Yuririhapúndaro and Pénjamo areas in 1522. San Miguel el Grande was founded in 1555 and the Villa de León in 1576.
Guanajuato became an intendancy in 1786.

eras.polity: War of Independence — Hidalgo's forces took the Alhóndiga
eras.note: Hidalgo's forces reached Guanajuato on 28 September 1810 and overwhelmed the Alhóndiga de Granaditas after two days. Guanajuato declared independence on 8 July 1821.
Guanajuato's admission as a state is dated 20 December 1823 or 1824 depending on the source.
Civil registration dates from 28 July 1859, kept by municipio.

regions.label: Michoacán and Guerrero
regions.sub: Morelia, Pátzcuaro, Uruapan, Acapulco, Taxco, Chilpancingo

eras.polity: New Spain — conquest of the Purépecha lands and the Pacific coast
eras.note: Spanish forces entered the Guerrero region in 1521 and Nuño de Guzmán killed the Purépecha ruler Tanganxoan II in 1530. The diocese of Michoacán dates from 1536 and Pátzcuaro was founded by Vasco de Quiroga in 1538.
Viceroy Mendoza founded Valladolid as the provincial capital in 1541; records before the later renaming are under Valladolid.

eras.polity: Michoacán a separate province — Acapulco the Pacific port
eras.note: Michoacán became a province separate from Mexico in 1602, and Acapulco was the main western port of New Spain, where the Manila galleon called each year.

eras.polity: State of Michoacán; Guerrero's lands in the States of Mexico, Puebla and Michoacán
eras.note: Michoacán became a state on 22 December 1823 or 31 January 1824, depending on the source. The Guerrero area was divided among the State of Mexico, Puebla and Michoacán.

eras.polity: Michoacán and the State of Guerrero (1849)
eras.note: Guerrero was admitted on 27 October 1849 from the districts of Acapulco, Chilapa and Taxco (State of Mexico), Tlapa (Puebla) and Coyuca (Michoacán), so earlier events in those districts sit with those states. Civil registration there is kept at district level.

regions.label: Guatemala (the Audiencia and Captaincy General)
regions.sub: Guatemala City, Antigua Guatemala, Quetzaltenango, Flores, Puerto Barrios

eras.note: Pedro de Alvarado led the conquest from 1524. The Audiencia of Guatemala was set up in 1543 with jurisdiction over most of Central America except Panama. Catholic parish registers run from the mid-1500s and are held in local parishes and in the Archivo General de Centro América and the Archdiocesan archive in Guatemala City.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Captaincy General of Guatemala
eras.note: From 1609 the governor and president of the Audiencia also held the title of captain general. The capital moved from Antigua to the present Guatemala City after the 1776 order to abandon Antigua. Spanish control was completed with the conquest of Nojpetén, in the Petén, in 1697.

eras.polity: Independence, then the First Mexican Empire
eras.note: The Act of Independence of Central America was signed on 15 September 1821. The Consultive Junta voted for annexation to the Mexican Empire on 5 January 1822, and the region left Mexico in July 1823 (Chiapas stayed with Mexico).

eras.polity: United Provinces / Federal Republic of Central America
eras.note: Guatemala City was the federal capital until 1834. The State of Los Altos, centred on the western highlands, existed 1838-1840. The federation's end is dated 17 April 1839 or to the close of the 1838-1840 civil war, depending on the source.

eras.polity: State of Guatemala after the federation
eras.note: The federation collapsed in 1838-1840 and Guatemala became an independent republic in 1847.

Civil registration began in 1877, when it was separated from the Church. The civil registry books are now held by the Registro Nacional de las Personas (RENAP), which replaced the Civil Registry under a 2006 law.

regions.label: Belize (British Honduras)
regions.sub: Belize City, Belmopan, San Ignacio, Corozal, Punta Gorda

eras.note: Buccaneers cut logwood from the 1650s and the first permanent British settlement dates from the late 1710s. Settlers elected magistrates from 1738 and Burnaby's Code of 1765 set their regulations. The 1763 and 1783 treaties allowed logwood cutting while Spanish sovereignty stood.

eras.polity: British Settlement in the Bay of Honduras
eras.note: The 1786 Convention of London allowed timber cutting but kept Spain's sovereignty and barred fortifications, government and plantations. The Battle of St George's Caye was fought in 1798 and the settlement afterwards extended south to the Sarstoon River. Britain recognised Mexico in 1825 and Mexico gave up its claim in 1826; the Dallas-Clarendon Treaty of 1856 and the Anglo-Guatemalan Treaty of 1859 followed, and the western boundary dates from 1859.

The settlement was declared the colony of British Honduras in 1862 under a lieutenant governor subordinate to the governor of Jamaica, and a Crown colony constitution took effect in April 1871. The northern boundary with Mexico along the Rio Hondo was agreed in 1893 and finalised in 1897.
Internal self-government began in January 1964 and the colony's name changed to Belize in June 1973. Guatemala's claim to the territory continued throughout.

Full independence came on 21 September 1981 under the Belize Act 1981 without agreement from Guatemala, which recognised Belize's independence in 1992. In December 2008 the two countries agreed to submit the territorial dispute to the International Court of Justice.

regions.label: Honduras (including Mosquitia and the Bay Islands)
regions.sub: Tegucigalpa, San Pedro Sula, Comayagua, La Ceiba, Roatán

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Province of Honduras, Audiencia of Guatemala
eras.note: Columbus reached the coast in 1502 and the Spanish campaigns of Olid, Cortés and Alvarado followed. Mining drew the economy first to Gracias and later to Tegucigalpa. Pirates and British settlers contested the Caribbean coast, and Spain built the fort at San Fernando de Omoa in 1752.

The Bourbon reforms created the intendancy of Comayagua in 1786, covering Honduras. The Mosquito coast stayed outside Spanish control: under the 1786 Convention of London Britain agreed to evacuate its settlers there and Spain began settling the area in 1787.

eras.polity: Independence, then the First Mexican Empire
United Provinces / Federal Republic of Central America
eras.note: Honduras was a state of the federation from 1823; it declared itself independent in 1838.

eras.polity: State of Honduras — the British on the coast
eras.note: Britain recognised the Mosquito Kingdom as an independent state in 1837 and declared a protectorate over it in 1844. Britain occupied the Bay Islands in 1852-1854 (dated there) and returned them in 1859.

The Bay Islands and the northern part of the Mosquito coast passed to Honduras in 1859-1860 (the Wyke-Cruz or Comayagua treaty). The capital moved to Tegucigalpa in 1880. Parish birth registers for 1842-1881 are held by the Registro Nacional de las Personas in Tegucigalpa.

Civil registration began in 1881 and is kept by each city's civil registry; births from 1906 are also at the Archivo Nacional in Tegucigalpa. In 1960 the International Court of Justice granted the northern part of the disputed Mosquito territory to Honduras.

regions.label: El Salvador
regions.sub: San Salvador, Santa Ana, San Miguel, Sonsonate, La Unión

eras.note: Pedro de Alvarado failed in 1524 after the Pipil beat him at the battle of Acajutla, and returned in 1525 to bring the area under Spanish control. Indigo was the main export.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Intendancy of San Salvador
eras.note: The Bourbon reforms made San Salvador an intendancy in 1786. Independence movements broke out in the San Salvador and León intendancies in 1811 and were put down.

eras.polity: Independence, then the First Mexican Empire
eras.note: El Salvador joined the Mexican Empire after the 1821 declaration of independence.
The federal capital moved from Guatemala City to San Salvador in 1834. The federation dissolved in February 1841, when El Salvador was recognised as an independent republic.

eras.polity: Republic of El Salvador — civil registration
eras.note: Civil registration began in 1879; the original records are kept in each municipality.

regions.label: Nicaragua (including the Mosquito Reserve)
regions.sub: Managua, León, Granada, Bluefields, Puerto Cabezas

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Province of Nicaragua, Audiencia of Guatemala
eras.note: Francisco Hernández de Córdoba founded Granada and León in 1524, and the Spanish conquest was complete by 1529. The eruption of Momotombo destroyed the capital at León in 1610.
León became an intendancy in 1786. The Cortes of Cádiz grouped Nicaragua and Costa Rica as one province in 1812-1814 and again in 1820-1821.

eras.polity: Independence, then the First Mexican Empire
United Provinces / Federal Republic of Central America
eras.note: Nicaragua became an independent republic in 1838.

eras.polity: Republic of Nicaragua — the Mosquito protectorate
eras.note: Britain declared a protectorate over the Mosquito Kingdom in 1844. Miskito-British forces seized San Juan del Norte in 1848 and renamed it Greytown, and the American filibuster William Walker seized power in Nicaragua in 1856 and was driven out in 1857.

eras.polity: Republic of Nicaragua — the Mosquito Reserve
eras.note: The Treaty of Managua of 28 January 1860 transferred suzerainty over the coast to Nicaragua and created the Mosquito Reserve. Civil registration began in 1879 and its records are held by the Consejo Supremo Electoral in Managua.

eras.polity: Republic of Nicaragua — the coast incorporated
eras.note: The Mosquito Reserve was incorporated into Nicaragua on 20 November 1894. The United States occupied Nicaragua from 1912 to 1933.

regions.label: Costa Rica
regions.sub: San José, Cartago, Heredia, Alajuela, Limón

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Province of Costa Rica, Audiencia of Guatemala
eras.note: The first Spanish colony, Villa de Bruselas, was founded in 1524. Costa Rica stayed a poor, thinly settled province of the Captaincy General of Guatemala. It received no intendancy, and its governor handled civil and military matters.

eras.polity: Independence, then the First Mexican Empire
eras.note: Costa Rica joined the 1821 Central American declaration of independence and was briefly part of the Mexican Empire.

eras.polity: United Provinces / Federal Republic of Central America
eras.note: Costa Rica joined the federation in 1823. At the Battle of Ochomogo in 1823 republican forces defeated those who favoured Mexico, and the capital moved to San José. Costa Rica seceded in 1838.
Costa Rica declared full independence from the federation in 1848.

eras.polity: Republic of Costa Rica — civil registration
eras.note: Civil registration began in 1888; the Civil Registry archive of the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones holds it.

regions.label: Panama
regions.sub: Panama City, Colón, David, Portobelo, Bocas del Toro

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Audiencia of Panama, then New Granada
eras.note: Panama City was founded on 15 August 1519 and the Real Audiencia of Panama was established in 1538. Panama was not part of the Captaincy General of Guatemala. Henry Morgan sacked the original city in 1671 and it was rebuilt on a nearby peninsula in 1673. The isthmus came under the Viceroyalty of New Granada, dated 1713, 1717 or 1739 depending on the passage.

eras.polity: Gran Colombia — Department of the Isthmus
eras.note: The national assembly declared independence from Spain on 28 November 1821 and chose to join Gran Colombia. Panama separated in September 1830 and rejoined what was left of the republic in early 1831.
The Free State of the Isthmus was formed in 1841 and reunified with New Granada on 31 December 1841. The Mallarino-Bidlack Treaty of 1846 gave the United States transit rights across the isthmus.

eras.polity: State of Panama within New Granada, the Granadine Confederation and Colombia
eras.note: The State of Panama was created on 27 February 1855 within New Granada. The Granadine Confederation replaced New Granada in 1858 and became the United States of Colombia in 1863. The French canal works began in 1881 or 1882, depending on the passage, and collapsed by 1889.

Panama separated from Colombia on 3 November 1903, and the United States built the canal in 1904-1914. Civil registration officially began on 15 April 1914, with mayors recording events locally until a National Civil Registry was created in 1974.
The canal and the remaining US bases were handed to Panama on 31 December 1999.

regions.label: Cuba
regions.sub: Havana, Santiago de Cuba, Camagüey, Trinidad, Pinar del Río

eras.note: Diego Velázquez left Hispaniola in 1511 to found the first Spanish settlement, at Baracoa; the present city of Havana was founded in 1519. The Archivo General de Indias holds the Papeles de Cuba, the records of the Spanish colonies across the Caribbean.
Britain occupied Havana in 1762 and returned it to Spain under the Peace of Paris of 1763 in exchange for Florida.

Spain agreed in 1817 to end the slave trade from 1820. The Ten Years' War ran from 10 October 1868 to the Pact of Zanjón on 10 February 1878, and a new war began on 24 February 1895. Slavery ended in 1880 or 1886 depending on the passage. Civil registration began in 1885; the Registro Civil in Havana holds it.
The Treaty of Paris was signed on 10 December 1898 and the United States took over government on 1 January 1899. Constituent Assembly elections were held on 15 September 1900.
The Republic of Cuba dates from 20 May 1902, when United States military government ended. The Platt Amendment, passed in 1901, let the United States intervene in Cuban affairs.

regions.label: Haiti (Saint-Domingue)
regions.sub: Port-au-Prince, Cap-Haïtien, Les Cayes, Jacmel, Jérémie

eras.note: Columbus landed on the island in 1492. Spain ceded the western part to France in 1697.

Saint-Domingue became France's richest colony. FamilySearch indexes French colonial civil registers for Saint-Domingue (1666-1809). The originals are reported to be at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence, with the alphabetical tables at CARAN.

An uprising of enslaved people began in 1791, traditionally dated 14 August. Slavery was abolished in 1793-1794, Napoleon sent an invasion force in 1802, and Haitian forces won the battle of Vertières in 1803. Independence was declared on 1 January 1804.

eras.polity: Haiti — kingdom of the north (Christophe) and republic of the south (Pétion)
eras.note: The country was split between the two states until reunification in 1820.

Jean-Pierre Boyer reunified the country and occupied the Spanish-speaking east in 1822. France demanded an indemnity in 1825 in return for recognition. Faustin Soulouque declared himself emperor in 1849 and the republic was restored in 1859. Extracts of civil records are obtained from the Archives nationales d'Haïti in Port-au-Prince.

regions.label: Dominican Republic (Santo Domingo)
regions.sub: Santo Domingo, Santiago, Puerto Plata, La Romana, Samaná

eras.note: The colony became a declining Spanish outpost living on cattle and contraband trade. The Archivo General de Indias holds papers filed under Santo Domingo.

eras.polity: French rule under the Treaty of Basel
eras.note: France gained the whole island under the Treaty of Basel in 1795. Haitian forces briefly took the French-held east.
Spain regained control in 1809.
A brief independent state was declared in late 1821 before Haiti annexed the territory in 1822.
Haitian rule ended slavery in the east. The earliest surviving civil registry books date from 1823 (Bayaguana).
Independence was declared on 27 February 1844 by the Trinitarios led by Juan Pablo Duarte.

eras.polity: Spanish annexation and the Restoration War
eras.note: Pedro Santana returned the country to Spain in 1861. A guerrilla war forced Spain out by July 1865.
The United States occupied the country in 1916-1924. Under law 659 of 1944 one original civil register is sent each year to the Central Office of the Civil State.

regions.label: Puerto Rico
regions.sub: San Juan, Ponce, Mayagüez, Arecibo, Humacao

eras.note: Juan Ponce de León founded Caparra, the first European settlement, in 1508. The Burgos Laws of 1512 regulated the treatment of the Taíno.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Captaincy General of Puerto Rico
eras.note: The island was reorganised as a captaincy general in 1580. A royal decree of 1815 offered free land to settlers. The Grito de Lares rising was in 1868 and slavery was abolished in 1873. Before 1885 vital events were recorded in Catholic parish registers.
Civil registration began in early 1885; the Registro Demográfico de Puerto Rico preserves vital records. An Autonomous Charter of 1897 granted self-government.
The Treaty of Paris of December 1898 transferred the island to the United States. The Foraker Act of 1900 set up a civil government and the Jones Act of 1917 granted citizenship.
The constitution of the Commonwealth was approved in 1952.

regions.label: Jamaica
regions.sub: Kingston, Spanish Town, Montego Bay, Port Royal, Mandeville

eras.note: Juan de Esquivel founded Sevilla la Nueva, the first permanent European settlement, in 1509, and the capital moved to Villa de la Vega (now Spanish Town) in 1534.

English forces took the island in 1655 and the Treaty of Madrid in 1670 confirmed English possession. Church of England records begin as early as 1664, and the Diocese of Jamaica was established in 1824. Registers of enslaved people kept from 1813 to 1834 are in The National Archives at Kew (series T 71) and on Ancestry.
Slavery was formally abolished in 1834 and the apprenticeships ended on 1 August 1838. After the Morant Bay Rebellion of 1865 the planters voted to abolish their own assembly.

Jamaica became a Crown Colony in 1866 and the capital moved from Spanish Town to Kingston in 1872. Civil registration of births and deaths began on 1 April 1878 in all 14 parishes, with marriages from 1880; the Registrar General's Office is at Twickenham Park. A new constitution of 1944 brought limited self-government.

regions.label: The Bahamas
regions.sub: Nassau, Freeport, Marsh Harbour, Governor's Harbour, Matthew Town

eras.polity: Spanish claim — the Lucayan islands emptied
eras.note: Columbus landed at Guanahani on 12 October 1492. The Spanish removed most of the Lucayans as labourers by 1520, leaving the islands largely depopulated for about 130 years.

eras.polity: English and British settlement — Eleuthera and New Providence
eras.note: Bermudian settlers founded the first lasting colony on Eleuthera in 1648 and Nassau was founded as Charles Town in 1670. Spain burned the Eleuthera and New Providence settlements in 1684-1686 and New Providence was resettled from Jamaica in 1686. Woodes Rogers arrived as governor in July 1718.
Spain captured the islands in 1782 and a Loyalist expedition retook them in 1783. The Peace of Paris of 1783 ceded them to Britain in exchange for East Florida.

Loyalist land grants tripled the population and enslaved Africans were brought in for plantation labour. Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 and liberated Africans were resettled in the Bahamas.
Emancipation took effect in August 1834. The Bahamas gained self-government in 1964.

regions.label: Virgin Islands (Danish West Indies — St Croix, St Thomas, St John)
regions.sub: Charlotte Amalie, Christiansted, Frederiksted, Cruz Bay, Coral Bay

eras.polity: Danish West India and Guinea Company
eras.note: The Danish West India Company took possession of St Thomas on 25 May 1672. St John was established on 25 March 1718 and Denmark bought St Croix from France on 28 June 1733.
The company went bankrupt in 1754 and King Frederick V took direct control of the three islands.
Britain returned the islands to Denmark in April 1802.
The occupation began in December 1807 and ended on 20 November 1815.

Governor Peter von Scholten announced total emancipation on 3 July 1848. The Danish National Archives hold parish registers from three religious communities and census series from 1841 to 1911, and most of the colonial records are digitised on Arkivalieronline. Some records stayed in the islands after the last major transfer of archives to Denmark in 1919.

Denmark sold the islands to the United States under a treaty concluded on 17 January 1917 and the United States took possession on 31 March 1917. The 1920 federal census of the Virgin Islands is among the microfilmed NARA records.

regions.label: Northern Leeward Islands (St Kitts, Antigua, Sint Maarten, Montserrat)
regions.sub: Basseterre, St. John's, Philipsburg, Marigot, Plymouth

eras.note: Columbus anchored off Nevis on 11 November 1493.
Thomas Warner arrived in 1623-1624 and Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc in 1625. In 1627 they divided the island into four quarters, the English holding the middle half.

eras.polity: British Leeward Islands, French St Kitts and the Dutch-French partition of St Martin
eras.note: France and the Dutch Republic divided Saint Martin on 23 March 1648 under the Treaty of Concordia. The British Leeward Islands became a colony in 1671 with William Stapleton as first governor. The Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 gave the French part of St Kitts to Britain.

The Treaty of Versailles of 1783 finally recognised British rule of St Kitts. The Leewards federation was dissolved in 1816 and re-established in 1833. On Saint Martin the border has been stable since 1816, after 16 changes.

Emancipation was proclaimed on 1 August 1834 in St Kitts, followed by four years of apprenticeship. A Leeward Islands federation dated 1871 existed, and from 1883 St Kitts, Nevis and Anguilla shared one assembly. Dominica moved from the Leeward Islands to the Windward Islands colony in 1940.

eras.polity: West Indies Federation, then separate states and territories
eras.note: St Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla was part of the West Indies Federation in 1958-1962, Anguilla broke from the union in 1971 and the federation of St Kitts and Nevis became independent in 1983. Saint-Martin and Saint-Barthélemy were part of Guadeloupe until their separation, completed by 2007, and the Dutch part of Saint Martin became a constituent country in 2010. French civil registers for Saint-Martin from 1807 to 1874 are catalogued under Guadeloupe.

regions.label: Guadeloupe, Dominica, Martinique and St Lucia
regions.sub: Pointe-à-Pitre, Basse-Terre, Fort-de-France, Roseau, Castries

eras.note: Columbus named Guadeloupe in 1493 and landed on Martinique in 1502, but Spain largely ignored the island.

France began colonising in 1635 and Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc founded the settlement that became Saint-Pierre on Martinique. Britain captured Martinique in 1762 and France recovered it in the Treaty of Paris of 1763. Martinique's parish registers from 1666 and civil registers to 1909 are reported online at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer.
Britain occupied Martinique in 1794-1802 and 1809-1814, and the 1794 French decree abolishing slavery was never applied there. Slavery was abolished in 1848.

eras.polity: French colonies of Guadeloupe and Martinique
eras.note: The eruption of Mount Pelée in 1902 destroyed Saint-Pierre. Dominica and Saint Lucia lay in British colonies: the Windward Islands colony existed 1833-1960 and Dominica joined it from the Leeward Islands in 1940.
Martinique became an overseas department in 1946 and Guadeloupe followed in the same year.

regions.label: Barbados, Grenada and Trinidad and Tobago
regions.sub: Bridgetown, St. George's, Port of Spain, Scarborough, Kingstown

eras.polity: Spanish claim — Trinidad, with a Portuguese claim to Barbados
eras.note: Columbus sighted Trinidad in 1498 and claimed it for Spain, and Antonio de Berrío founded San José de Oruña in 1592. Portugal held a claim to Barbados from 1532 to 1620.

eras.polity: English Barbados, Spanish Trinidad and a contested Tobago
eras.note: England settled Barbados for good in 1627 and its House of Assembly dates from 1639. Tobago changed hands among the Dutch, Courlanders, English and French between 1628 and 1677. Trinidad stayed Spanish, and a Cédula of Population in 1783 drew French planters.

Britain captured Trinidad in 1797 and the Treaty of Amiens in 1802 formalised British rule. Tobago came under Britain by the Treaty of Paris of 1763 and, after later exchanges with France, again by the Treaty of Paris of 1814. Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807. Trinidad slave registers are in The National Archives at Kew (T 71/501-519).

Slavery ended in 1834 and Trinidad's apprenticeship ended on 1 August 1838. Indentured Indian labour was introduced from 1844. Barbados ceased to be part of the Windward Islands colony in 1885 and Tobago in 1889, when Trinidad and Tobago became a single unit on 1 January 1889.
The Windward Islands colony, originally Grenada, Saint Lucia and Saint Vincent, lasted until 1960. Barbados and Trinidad and Tobago were members of the West Indies Federation, 1958-1962.

eras.polity: Independent Trinidad and Tobago and Barbados
eras.note: Trinidad and Tobago became independent on 31 August 1962 and a republic on 1 August 1976. Barbados became independent on 30 November 1966 and a republic on 30 November 2021.

regions.label: Caribbean Colombia — Cartagena, Santa Marta, Barranquilla
regions.sub: Cartagena, Santa Marta, Barranquilla, Riohacha, Montería, Valledupar

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — provinces of Cartagena and Santa Marta, New Kingdom of Granada
eras.note: Cartagena was founded on 1 June 1533. The Audiencia of Santa Fe, created in 1549, had authority over the provinces of Santa Marta and Cartagena de Indias; the Inquisition opened a tribunal at Cartagena in 1610. The Archivo General de la Nación in Bogotá holds colonial-era material from 1541, and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville holds the records of the Council of the Indies and the Casa de la Contratación.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of New Granada
eras.note: The viceroyalty was created in 1717, suspended in 1723 and re-established on 20 August 1739. Santa Marta is listed in it for 1717-1723 and 1739-1821, and Cartagena de Indias until 1810.

eras.polity: Contested — Cartagena independent from 1811, Spanish reconquest 1815-16, patriot victory 1821
eras.note: Cartagena signed a declaration of independence on 11 November 1811, was besieged and retaken by Spanish forces in 1815-1816, and fell to patriot forces in 1821 after a siege that began in 1820. Santa Marta is listed in the viceroyalty until 1821, so the two ports changed hands on different dates.

Gran Colombia was proclaimed at Angostura on 17 December 1819 and given legal existence by the Constitution of Cúcuta on 30 August 1821. The union dissolved in late 1830 and was formally abolished in 1831.

eras.polity: Republic of New Granada (1831-58), Granadine Confederation (1858-63), United States of Colombia (1863-86)
eras.note: The former Department of Cundinamarca became the Republic of New Granada; the state was renamed in 1858 and again in 1863, so a record of these years can carry any of three national names. Civil registration began in 1865, but it was not adopted nationwide until 1888.

The country took the name Republic of Colombia in 1886 under a constitution that remained in force until 1991. Civil registration has been exclusively a State responsibility since Law 92 of 1938; before 1926 civil records were part of notarial records, and the Registraduría Nacional del Estado Civil now keeps the registers.

regions.label: Bogotá and the eastern Andes — Cundinamarca, Boyacá, Santander
regions.sub: Bogotá, Tunja, Bucaramanga, Cúcuta, Ibagué, Neiva, Villavicencio

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — New Kingdom of Granada, Audiencia of Santa Fe
eras.note: Bogotá was founded on 6 August 1538 by Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada as capital of the New Kingdom of Granada (one historian dates his claim to the Muisca capital to 1537). The Audiencia of Santa Fe was created by royal decree on 17 July 1549, and some accounts date its installation to 1550. FamilySearch's Colombian Catholic church collection begins in 1576.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of New Granada
eras.note: Santa Fe was part of the Viceroyalty of New Granada in 1717-1723 and again from 1739; the viceroyalty was suspended in 1723 and re-established on 20 August 1739. The Audiencia of Santa Fe was disestablished in 1810.

eras.polity: Contested — juntas from 1810, Spanish reconquest from 1816
eras.note: Independence was declared on 20 July 1810. Spanish forces reconquered New Granada from 3 September 1816 and re-established the Audiencia of Santa Fe until 1819, when the Battle of Boyacá on 7 August 1819 gave the patriots control.
The 1821 Constitution of Cúcuta created three departments, Cundinamarca (Bogotá), Venezuela and Quito; in 1824 they were divided into twelve smaller departments. The union dissolved in late 1830.

eras.polity: Republic of New Granada (1831-58), Granadine Confederation (1858-63), United States of Colombia (1863-86)
eras.note: New Granada was formed from the old Department of Cundinamarca. The national name changed to the Granadine Confederation in 1858 and the United States of Colombia in 1863.

Law 57 of 1887 allowed civil status to be proved with a priest-issued baptism, marriage or death certificate, so church certificates continue to stand in for civil entries in this period. The Thousand Days' War of 1899-1902 was a civil war between Conservatives and Liberals.

regions.label: Antioquia, the Cauca and the Pacific coast — Medellín, Popayán, Cali, Pasto
regions.sub: Medellín, Manizales, Popayán, Cali, Pasto, Buenaventura, Quibdó

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Antioquia (New Kingdom of Granada) and the Governorate of Popayán
eras.note: The Audiencia of Santa Fe was created in 1549. In the later Viceroyalty's own listing, Antioquia belongs to the New Kingdom of Granada but Popayán belongs to the Kingdom of Quito, so records for the south-west may follow Quito rather than Santa Fe.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of New Granada
eras.note: The viceroyalty was created in 1717, suspended in 1723 and re-established in 1739. Antioquia is listed in it for 1717-1723 and 1739-1810, and Popayán for 1717-1723 and 1739-1821.

eras.polity: Contested — juntas from 1810, Spanish reconquest from 1816, Popayán royalist to 1821
eras.note: Independence was declared on 20 July 1810 and Spanish forces reconquered New Granada from 3 September 1816. The viceroyalty's listing keeps Antioquia only until 1810 and again for 1816-1819, but Popayán until 1821.
The 1821 constitution created the departments of Cundinamarca, Venezuela and Quito; in 1824 these were divided into twelve smaller departments.
New Granada was formed from the former Department of Cundinamarca after Gran Colombia dissolved.

eras.polity: States of Antioquia (1856) and Cauca (1857), in the United States of Colombia from 1863
eras.note: Antioquia was created as a state on 11 June 1856 and Cauca on 15 June 1857; both joined the United States of Colombia on 8 May 1863. A record of these years may have been created by a state government rather than the national one.
The union of states ended in 1886, when the country took the name Republic of Colombia. FamilySearch's Colombian baptism collection runs 1630-1950, marriages 1750-1960 and deaths 1770-1930.

regions.label: Caracas, the central coast, the Llanos and the east — Cumaná, Margarita, Guayana
regions.sub: Caracas, Valencia, Barquisimeto, Coro, Cumaná, Margarita, Ciudad Bolívar

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — provinces of Venezuela, Nueva Andalucía (Cumaná) and Guayana
eras.note: Spanish colonisation of the mainland began in 1502 with Cumaná; its founding is dated 1521 or 1523 in different accounts. Nueva Andalucía was established as a province in 1537 with Cumaná as capital. The Welser family held colonial rights in the west from 1528 to 1546.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of New Granada (Venezuelan provinces)
eras.note: The province joined the Viceroyalty of New Granada in 1717, which was suspended in 1723 and re-established in 1739. The Guipuzcoan Company gained a trade monopoly in 1726.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Captaincy General of Venezuela
eras.note: The Captaincy General was created on 8 September 1777 and joined the provinces of Venezuela (Caracas), Cumaná, Guayana, Maracaibo, Margarita and Trinidad; Trinidad was lost to Britain in 1797. A separate Audiencia of Caracas followed in 1786.

eras.polity: Contested — First Republic (1811), Spanish reconquest, Second Republic (1813)
eras.note: Seven of the ten provinces declared independence on 5 July 1811. The First Republic fell in 1812 and Bolívar re-established the Republic in 1813; independence was secured in 1821.

The 1821 Gran Colombia constitution created the Department of Venezuela with its seat at Caracas; in 1824 the departments were split into twelve. Puerto Cabello, the last royalist stronghold, fell in November 1823.

Venezuela became a separate sovereign country in 1830 (some accounts say 1831). Civil registration began in 1865; registers are kept by the local civil registry office of each municipality, and you need the town and an approximate year to find them.

regions.label: Maracaibo and the Venezuelan Andes — Zulia, Mérida, Trujillo, Táchira, Barinas
regions.sub: Maracaibo, Mérida, San Cristóbal, Trujillo, Valera, Barinas

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Maracaibo and Mérida under the New Kingdom of Granada
eras.note: Maracaibo was founded in 1529, during the Welser concession (1528-1546). Mérida formed part of the Audiencia of Santa Fe from its origins until 1777. FamilySearch's registers for the Diocese of San Cristóbal start in 1601 and for the Archdiocese of Mérida in 1654.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of New Granada
eras.note: Mérida depended on the Viceroyalty of New Granada until 1777, and in judicial matters Maracaibo answered to the Audiencia of Santa Fe until the same year.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Captaincy General of Venezuela
eras.note: The royal decree of 8 September 1777 separated Maracaibo from the Audiencia of Santa Fe in judicial matters and kept it attached to the Captaincy General and Intendancy of Caracas; accounts differ on how the decree treated Mérida. Maracaibo and Barinas asked to return to New Granada in 1778, and the Audiencia of Caracas was created in 1786.

eras.polity: Contested — First and Second Republics, Spanish reconquest, royalist resistance to 1823
eras.note: Seven of ten provinces declared independence on 5 July 1811. Royalist resistance continued in the west: a naval victory on Lake Maracaibo on 24 July 1823 was followed by the fall of Puerto Cabello in November 1823.
Venezuela formed one of the three original departments of Gran Colombia in 1821; in 1824 the departments were split into twelve smaller ones.
Parish registers in the Andes are held by dioceses and local parishes: earlier registers can be at the diocese, and more recent ones are kept in the parish.

regions.label: Ecuador — Quito, Cuenca, Guayaquil
regions.sub: Quito, Guayaquil, Cuenca, Loja, Esmeraldas, Ambato

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of Peru (Quito and Guayaquil)
eras.note: San Francisco de Quito was established in 1534. Guayaquil was founded in 1533, retaken by its inhabitants, and re-established in 1537.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Audiencia of Quito, Viceroyalty of Peru
eras.note: The Audiencia of Quito was created by royal decree on 29 August 1563, with a district that included Quito, Cuenca, Loja and Guayaquil; it was effectively autonomous because the viceroy was far away. FamilySearch's Ecuadorian Catholic church collection begins in 1565.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of New Granada, Audiencia of Quito
eras.note: Quito is listed in the Viceroyalty of New Granada for 1717-1723, when the viceroyalty was suspended and the Audiencia passed back to Peru, and again from 1739. Guayaquil is listed in the viceroyalty only for 1763-1803.

eras.polity: Contested — Quito junta (1809), Guayaquil independent (1820), liberation (1822)
eras.note: After the Quito revolution of August 1809 the Audiencia was independent for about three years before Spain reannexed it in 1812. Guayaquil proclaimed independence in October 1820, and Quito was liberated in 1822.

eras.polity: Gran Colombia — the former Audiencia of Quito
eras.note: Quito joined Gran Colombia in 1822 and the Audiencia's territory was divided into departments in 1824.

In May 1830 Quito notables dissolved the union with Gran Colombia and Ecuador became a separate state. Civil registration did not begin until 1900, so for these years the Catholic parish registers are the main record.

Civil registration began in 1900. Records are kept by each municipality's civil registry, with copies at the Dirección General del Registro Civil in Quito. Ecuador and Peru fought a war in 1941 and signed the Rio Protocol in 1942.

regions.label: Lima and northern Peru — Lima, Trujillo, Piura, Cajamarca
regions.sub: Lima, Callao, Trujillo, Chiclayo, Piura, Cajamarca, Huancayo

eras.polity: Spanish conquest — Pizarro at Cajamarca and the founding of Lima
eras.note: Spanish forces seized Atahualpa at Cajamarca on 16 November 1532, and Pizarro founded Lima on 18 January 1535 as the City of Kings.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of Peru (Lima the seat)
eras.note: The Viceroyalty of Peru was established by the New Laws of 20 November 1542. FamilySearch lists a regional Lima collection covering 1683-1998.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of Peru under the intendancies
eras.note: Intendancies were created across Peru between 1783 and 1786 under the Bourbon reforms, so administrative papers of these years may be filed by intendancy rather than by the older districts.

San Martín proclaimed independence at Lima on 28 July 1821; the royalists were defeated at Ayacucho on 9 December 1824 and the viceroyalty was dissolved on 30 December 1824, though Callao held out until 1826.

The Confederation was founded by decree on 28 October 1836 and formalised by the Pact of Tacna on 1 May 1837, with three member states (North Peru, South Peru and Bolivia). It ended with the defeat at Yungay on 20 January 1839, and Gamarra declared it dissolved on 25 August 1839.
Death registration began in Lima in 1857; Lima's municipal archives hold death registers for 1857-1867. The guano era lasted from 1845 to 1866.
The War of the Pacific lasted from 1879 to 1883, and the occupation of Lima and the Peruvian resistance are dated 1881-1883.

In most municipalities births and marriages are registered from 1886 and deaths from 1857, and a civil law of 1892 made registration mandatory. The General Archive of the Nation in Lima holds Lima and Callao birth, marriage and death records up to 1997 (some to 1999); the Archivo de la Corte Suprema holds duplicates.

regions.label: Southern Peru — Cusco, Arequipa, Puno, Ayacucho
regions.sub: Cusco, Arequipa, Puno, Ayacucho, Juliaca, Moquegua, Abancay

eras.polity: Spanish conquest — Cuzco re-founded as a Spanish settlement
eras.note: Pizarro had re-founded Cuzco as a Spanish settlement by 23 March 1534.
In 1776 the Audiencia of Charcas passed to the new Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. The Puno district lay under Charcas, which matters for Puno records before 1796.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of Peru, intendancies and the Audiencia of Cuzco
eras.note: After the Túpac Amaru II rebellion (1780-1783) the Audiencia of Cuzco was ordered established on 26 February 1787. In 1796 the Intendancy of Puno moved under the Viceroyalty of Peru, and in 1821 the Intendancy of Arequipa was added to the Audiencia's district.
Independence was proclaimed on 28 July 1821; the Audiencia of Cuzco was definitively dissolved in 1825, after Ayacucho (9 December 1824).
The Confederation, with Tacna as capital, set up North Peru, South Peru and Bolivia as member states and lasted until the defeat at Yungay on 20 January 1839.
FamilySearch's Cusco civil registration collection runs 1889-1997. Births and marriages are registered from 1886 in most municipalities.

regions.label: Tacna and Arica — the 1879-84 War of the Pacific
regions.sub: Tacna, Arica, Candarave, Putre

eras.note: The Viceroyalty of Peru was established by the New Laws of 20 November 1542 and was dissolved on 30 December 1824.
Independence was proclaimed at Lima on 28 July 1821.
The Pact of Tacna formalised the Confederation on 1 May 1837, and Tacna was its capital.
Tacna and Arica were Peruvian until the War of the Pacific.

eras.polity: Chilean occupation and administration (Tacna and Arica)
eras.note: Chilean forces won the Battle of Tacna on 26 May 1880 and took Arica on 7 June 1880. The Treaty of Ancón (20 October 1883) left Tacna and Arica under Chilean control for a fixed period, with a plebiscite to follow; it was never held. FamilySearch records Tacna civil registration under Chile as births from 1884 and marriages and deaths from 1885.

eras.polity: Tacna to Peru, Arica to Chile
eras.note: The Treaty of Lima, signed on 3 June 1929 and in force from 28 August 1929, gave Tacna to Peru while Chile retained Arica. Records from this date for the two cities belong to different national systems.

regions.label: La Paz, Oruro, Potosí, Sucre and Tarija — the Altiplano and the Charcas valleys
regions.sub: La Paz, Oruro, Potosí, Sucre, Tarija, Uyuni

eras.note: Before registers. Western Bolivia was part of the Inca province of Qullasuyu from 1438 and the Spanish conquest ran from 1524 to 1538; La Paz was founded in 1548.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Audiencia of Charcas, Viceroyalty of Peru
eras.note: The Audiencia of Charcas, seated at La Plata (now Sucre), is dated 4 September 1559 in one account and 1558 in another. The Archivo y Biblioteca Nacionales de Bolivia in Sucre was created in 1883 on the Audiencia's documentation, and its catalogued holdings include the Audiencia's papers for 1561-1825 and the public deeds of La Plata for 1548-1825. FamilySearch's Bolivian baptism collection begins in 1560.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (Upper Peru)
eras.note: In 1776 Charcas passed from the Viceroyalty of Peru to the new Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, where it was known as Upper Peru. Túpac Amaru II and Túpac Catari led major Indigenous revolts in 1780-1783.

eras.polity: Contested — Upper Peru in the independence wars
eras.note: Charcas formed juntas in 1809 that deposed the Audiencia's judges; they were suppressed in 1810 and the Audiencia was restored in 1816 under the Viceroy of Peru. Independence was declared on 6 August 1825.
The Republic of Bolivia was created from the territory of the Audiencia of Charcas on 6 August 1825 and named for Simón Bolívar.
Bolivia was one of the Confederation's three member states, with North Peru and South Peru, from 1836 until its end in 1839.
In the War of the Pacific (1879-1884) Bolivia lost its Pacific coastline to Chile. FamilySearch's Bolivian marriage collection runs 1630-1940.

Civil registration of births, marriages and deaths began in 1940 according to FamilySearch, though its register headings say 1898. A 1945 law let Bolivians born before 1940 who were not in the civil registry obtain a birth certificate with a baptismal record or witnesses; the Órgano Electoral Plurinacional in La Paz is the contact office.

regions.label: Cochabamba, Santa Cruz and the eastern lowlands of Bolivia
regions.sub: Cochabamba, Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Trinidad, Camiri, Puerto Suárez

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Audiencia of Charcas (Santa Cruz de la Sierra)
eras.note: The 1680 Recopilación describes the boundaries of the Audiencia of Charcas, and they include Santa Cruz de la Sierra. The Archivo y Biblioteca Nacionales de Bolivia in Sucre holds the Audiencia's papers for 1561-1825.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire — Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (Upper Peru)
eras.note: In 1776 Charcas moved to the new Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata and became known as Upper Peru.

eras.polity: Contested — Upper Peru in the independence wars
eras.note: The 1809 juntas were suppressed in 1810 and the Audiencia was restored in 1816 under the Viceroy of Peru; Bolivia declared independence on 6 August 1825.
The Chaco War with Paraguay (1932-1935) ended in defeat for Bolivia. Bolivia was one of the three member states of the Peru–Bolivian Confederation in 1836-1839.

FamilySearch dates the start of civil registration to 1940, with register headings reading 1898; baptismal records stand in for births before 1940 under a 1945 law. The National Revolution of 9 April 1952 brought land reform.

regions.label: Guyana — Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice
regions.sub: Georgetown, New Amsterdam, Linden, Bartica, Lethem

eras.note: The Dutch set up a trading post on the Essequibo in 1616; the West India Company took control of Essequibo in 1621, Berbice was founded in 1627 and Demerara was settled in 1741. From 1792 Demerara and Essequibo were a united colony under direct Dutch government. The Nationaal Archief in The Hague holds a digital duplicate of the surviving records of the three colonies (about 1674-1814); the originals are in the National Archives of Guyana in Georgetown.

eras.polity: British occupation of the Dutch colonies
eras.note: Britain took the colonies in 1796, the Treaty of Amiens returned them to the Dutch, and British forces seized them again in 1803. The London Convention of 1814 formally ceded them to Britain; the UK National Archives series C.O. 116 includes Dutch West India Company papers of 1686-1792.

eras.polity: British — Berbice and Demerara-Essequibo as separate colonies
eras.note: The Demerara rebellion of enslaved people took place in 1823. Berbice and Demerara-Essequibo were united as British Guiana in 1831.

Slavery was abolished between 1833 and 1838, and indentured workers from India arrived from 1838 until the system ended in 1917. An 1899 arbitral award gave Britain about 94 per cent of the territory disputed with Venezuela, and both sides accepted the boundary in 1905.
Guyana became independent on 26 May 1966 and a Co-operative Republic in 1970. Guyana filed a case against Venezuela at the International Court of Justice in March 2018 over the border.

regions.label: Suriname — Paramaribo and the Dutch plantation colony
regions.sub: Paramaribo, Nieuw Nickerie, Albina, Moengo

eras.polity: Dutch trading post and a failed English attempt
eras.note: Before registers. The Dutch set up a trading post on the Suriname River in 1613, and English settlers under Captain Marshall attempted a colony in 1630 that failed.
Lord Willoughby, governor of Barbados, funded an English settlement in 1650, established by Major Anthony Rowse.

Dutch ships captured the English settlement in 1667 and renamed it Fort Zeelandia, and the Treaty of Breda of 31 July 1667 confirmed Dutch control. The Treaty of Westminster formalised the arrangement in 1674, and the Society of Suriname was set up in 1683.
Britain occupied Suriname in 1799, and it returned to Dutch rule in 1816.

The Dutch abolished slavery in 1863, but freed workers stayed bound to plantation work until 1873; labourers were then brought from India (1873-1916) and later from the Dutch East Indies, mainly Java. The Nationaal Archief Suriname holds civil registration entries for Paramaribo, some from 1847, which are indexed on Open Archives.

eras.polity: Suriname — self-government within the Kingdom of the Netherlands
eras.note: Suriname gained self-government within the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1954.
Suriname became independent on 25 November 1975.

regions.label: French Guiana — Cayenne, Kourou, Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni
regions.sub: Cayenne, Kourou, Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, Sinnamary

eras.polity: Before registers — a failed Tuscan expedition
eras.note: Before registers. The Grand Duchy of Tuscany's expedition of 1608 failed after its sponsor died.

The French settled in 1643 and again in 1664, the Dutch held Cayenne from 1658, and the English seized the area in 1667 before the Treaty of Breda returned it to France that year. The Archives nationales d'outre-mer hold a third copy of the parish and civil registers of the former colonies, and their Cayenne tribunal fonds covers 1677-1881.

eras.polity: French Guiana after the 1763 Treaty of Paris
eras.note: After the Treaty of Paris of 1763 the settlers sent by Louis XV largely died. Republican prisoners were deported there in 1794 and 1797.
An Anglo-Portuguese force took the colony in 1809, and France regained it under the 1814 Treaty of Paris, though a Portuguese presence lasted until 1817.

Slavery was abolished in 1848 and convicts began to arrive in 1852; a law of 1885 sent habitual offenders there as relégués. The original registers sorted by commune are in the territorial archives (series 1E), where the listed ranges for Cayenne begin in 1828.
Guiana became an overseas département in 1946 and the penal colonies were formally closed in 1951. Kourou was chosen as a launch site in 1964.

regions.label: Bahia and Sergipe — Salvador, the Recôncavo, Ilhéus
regions.sub: Salvador, Cachoeira, Ilhéus, Porto Seguro, Feira de Santana, Aracaju

eras.note: Before registers. Cabral landed at what is now Porto Seguro in 1500. The Bahia captaincy was the first of the hereditary captaincies to fail and its lands reverted to the Crown.

eras.polity: Colony of Brazil — Governorate General, Salvador its capital
eras.note: Salvador was founded in 1549 and was the colony's administrative capital until 1763. Dutch forces held Salvador from May 1624 until a Spanish-Portuguese force retook it on 30 April 1625. FamilySearch's Bahia church-record collections start as early as 1598 (an overall range, individual parishes vary); the Conselho Ultramarino fonds, the Crown's overseas council papers, is in the Arquivo Histórico Ultramarino in Lisbon.

eras.polity: Captaincy of Bahia (Sergipe split off in 1820)
eras.note: Sergipe was separated from Bahia in 1820, so Sergipe events before that year belong to the Bahia captaincy. Espírito Santo had become independent of Bahia in 1799.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of Bahia
